slides.title: Course objectives
notes:
The objectives cover features, configuration and maintenance of enterprise LAN switches. The 2007 platforms (SecureStack and Matrix N with DFE-P) are the historical reference; the same roadmap applies today to Extreme Switch Engine and Fabric Engine (the current names of the former ExtremeXOS and VOSS) and to other systems such as Cisco IOS XE, Aruba AOS-CX, Junos, RouterOS, Arista EOS and Huawei VRP. In operations, knowing the concept lets you move between CLIs quickly. Tip: keep a command-equivalence table for the end of the day.

slides.title: Course objectives
notes:
These are the practical outcomes of Day 01: access the device, upgrade the firmware, manage configuration files, return to factory defaults and recover access when the password is unknown. Each item maps to a lab of the day. In operations, the last three items are what save you during a device swap or a lost access. Tip: point out that password recovery requires physical access to the device, which is also a form of protection.

slides.title: From 2007 to 2026: what changed
notes:
Set the scene: the original course (2007) was written for the Enterasys line; vendors and products have changed names and owners since. Every event below was checked against an official source.

2007: Original course for the Enterasys line (SecureStack and Matrix)
2013: Extreme Networks completes the Enterasys acquisition (31 Oct)
2017: Extreme completes the Avaya networking purchase: VSP line and VOSS (14 Jul)
2021: Extreme Management Center (formerly NetSight) end of sale; successor: ExtremeCloud IQ Site Engine
2022: VOSS 8.6 is renamed Fabric Engine on universal hardware
2024: End of service for the S and K chassis (Enterasys EOS)
2025: HPE completes the Juniper Networks acquisition (2 Jul)
2026: This edition: the 2007 legacy and the current CLI of eight vendors

slides.title: Cisco IOS XE
notes:
Profile of Cisco IOS XE. Each field was checked against the official documentation listed below.

IOS XE 26.1.x: Release notes: 26.1.1 on 10 Apr 2026, 26.1.2 on 5 Aug 2026. Extended Support, 48 months. Not in the recommended list (4 Sep 2026: 17.18.4, 17.15.6). 17.18.x supported to 30 Mar 2030. Time-based: year.release.maintenance (26.1.1, 26.1.2, 26.2.1). Two releases per year; all Extended Support, 48 months from GA. All insecure CLI is blocked by default; the override is system mode insecure, added automatically on upgrade if insecure config exists (B01, B05). Telnet on lines, ip http server, TFTP/FTP/RCP and SNMPv1/v2c are insecure: use SSH, ip http secure-server, SCP and SNMPv3 (B01, B05). 26.1 image: cat9k_iosxe.26.01.01.SPA.bin (and the _npe variant); install add file activate commit is the same as 17.18 (B06). ROMMON is reached with the Mode button (2 to 3 presses while the System LED blinks), not Ctrl-C (B04). In the 26.x guide, ntp server and ntp peer accept version 1 to 4, default 4 (17.18: 1 to 3, default 3) (B02).

slides.title: CLI families: what you learn here carries over to other vendors
notes:
Skill-transfer map: each vendor is placed in the most similar CLI family, based on three commands checked in official documentation (enter configuration, access port in VLAN 10, save). Someone who knows the family picks up the other quickly.

Dell PowerSwitch (data center S/Z-series and N3200-ON): configure terminal, switchport access vlan and write memory are the same as Cisco IOS XE; only the interface naming differs (interface ethernet 1/1/14).
Dell PowerSwitch N-series campus (N1100-ON, N2200-ON, N3000 family): console# prompt with enable/configure, interface Gi1/0/1, switchport access vlan and write memory or copy running-config startup-config: syntax nearly identical to IOS.
RUCKUS ICX: device# prompt, enable, configure terminal and write memory are the IOS ones; the difference is that a port joins the VLAN from VLAN mode (untagged ethernet 1/1/1), not from interface mode.
NETGEAR M4250 / M4300 / M4350: User EXEC, Privileged EXEC, Global Config and Interface Config modes with switchport mode access, switchport access vlan and write memory: IOS-style syntax; interfaces are numbered 1/0/1.
Ruijie RG-S series: enable, configure terminal, interface, switchport mode access and switchport access vlan are identical to IOS; saving uses write (or write memory), as in classic IOS.
H3C campus switches: system-view to enter configuration, a per-object view for the interface, port link-type access and save: the same lineage as Huawei VRP (only the keyword differs, port access vlan versus port default vlan).
Alcatel-Lucent Enterprise OmniSwitch: Like EXOS, the CLI is flat with no configuration mode: the port joins the VLAN from the VLAN command itself (vlan 100 members port ... untagged, similar to configure vlan X add ports ... untagged) and saving is one command (write memory, similar to save configuration).
Hirschmann (Belden) HiOS: User/Privileged EXEC and Configuration modes, interface 1/1 and save resemble IOS; the port joins the VLAN with vlan participation include and vlan pvid, and the VLAN is created in vlan database.
Cisco Catalyst IE3400 / IE9300 Rugged: It is Cisco IOS XE itself: the same commands as Catalyst 9000, so the course's IOS XE twin applies unchanged.
NVIDIA Spectrum (Cumulus Linux / NVUE): NVUE runs in the Linux shell (cumulus@switch:~$ nv set ...) with no configuration mode; the pending-config logic with nv config diff, nv config apply and --confirm resembles Junos commit, but the syntax is its own.
SONiC (open source, SONiC Foundation): The community CLI is the Linux shell (admin@sonic:~$) with sudo config and show commands that write to ConfigDB; there is no configuration mode and no syntax shared with the eight families.
Cisco Meraki MS (cloud-managed switches): MS is configured in the cloud (Dashboard) through a port form; there is no config mode and no save command: the Update button pushes the change to the switch. The local status page only allows minimal changes to get the switch online.
Ubiquiti UniFi switches: The port is configured in the UniFi Network application (native VLAN and tagged VLAN management), with no config mode and no save command. Ubiquiti describes SSH only as an advanced option for support, not as the way to configure the switch.
TP-Link Omada switches: In standalone mode the CLI has the IOS structure: privileged mode, configure, interface gigabitEthernet 1/0/1, a (config-if) prompt and copy running-config startup-config. The difference is per-port VLAN: switchport general allowed vlan ... untagged plus switchport pvid, instead of switchport access vlan. Once a controller adopts the switch, local configuration is no longer accepted.

slides.title: Cloud-managed switching: the other operating model
notes:
Part of the market (Meraki, UniFi, Omada and the course vendors' own cloud platforms) is run from a dashboard, not a CLI. The networking reasoning is the same; what changes is where the configuration lives. The cards summarise the facts below, checked on official pages.

Cisco Meraki MS: Dashboard configuration and local status page: MS is configured in the Dashboard: on Switching > Monitor > Switch ports the administrator selects ports, clicks Edit, sets the type (access or trunk) and VLAN, and Update 'will instantly push the changes' to the switch. The local status page (switch.meraki.com) offers only connection info, uplink IP, support data, packet capture and limited port changes; Meraki warns that local changes are overwritten by the Dashboard configuration.
Cisco Meraki Dashboard API: The Dashboard API is REST over HTTPS (base https://api.meraki.com/api/v1, for example the /switch/ports resource) and authenticates with 'Authorization: Bearer <API key>'. The limit is 10 requests per second per organization (plus 10 extra in the first second) and 100 per second per source IP; when exceeded the API returns 429 with a Retry-After header.
Ubiquiti UniFi: UniFi Network application and control plane: A UniFi switch is managed by the UniFi Network application, which runs on a control plane: Cloud Gateway, CloudKey, UniFi OS Server (self-hosted, replacing the legacy UniFi Network Server) or Official UniFi Hosting (in Ubiquiti's cloud). UniFi Site Manager (unifi.ui.com) gives remote access and a multi-site view, and Ubiquiti says configuration and control stay on the local or chosen control plane, not in the cloud. If the server goes offline, devices keep running the last configuration.
Ubiquiti UniFi: official APIs: Ubiquiti offers the Site Manager API (unifi.ui.com, aggregated view of all sites) and per-application local APIs; the Network API documentation is inside the application, at UniFi Network > Integrations, and covers devices (including switches), clients and traffic.
TP-Link Omada: controller options and platform names: Omada has three controller types: cloud-based (unlimited management scale with zero-touch provisioning), hardware (on-premises, no PC or server) and software (on-premises, no hardware cost). On the cloud page TP-Link lists Omada Central (a unified networking and surveillance platform), Omada Central Essentials (free) and the Omada Cloud-Based Controller, described as the networking module of Omada Central. The adoption article says a switch can be adopted by a hardware, software or cloud-based controller.
TP-Link Omada: standalone mode versus controller mode: An Omada switch can be configured directly by CLI/WebUI in standalone mode, but once a controller adopts it local configuration is disabled and everything goes through the controller. On firmware adapted to Controller v6.2, if the switch loses its controller the local WebUI becomes reachable again and SSH is enabled automatically after 30 minutes.
Extreme Networks: ExtremeCloud IQ and Extreme Platform ONE: Cloud management for Extreme switches is ExtremeCloud IQ: the product page says it supports access points, switches and SD-WAN and can be deployed in public cloud, private cloud or ExtremeCloud Edge. Extreme's site now features Extreme Platform ONE, which it describes as 'unifying networking, security, and AI', and lists ExtremeCloud IQ as a separate login entry.
Extreme Networks: ExtremeCloud IQ API: The ExtremeCloud IQ API follows the OpenAPI standard and RESTful design, and the developer portal offers a Swagger UI and SDKs (Java, JavaScript, Python, Go, C#) to manage, monitor and provision an ExtremeCloud IQ environment.
Cisco Catalyst switches: Meraki dashboard and Catalyst Center: Cisco offers cloud management for Catalyst through the Meraki dashboard: per the Meraki switches page, cloud-native IOS XE lets select Catalyst 9000 switches be onboarded and managed in the dashboard, and the Catalyst 9300-M has native cloud management. In parallel, Cisco Catalyst Center is the management tool named in the Catalyst IE data sheets.
HPE Aruba CX switches: HPE Aruba Central: The management platform is HPE Aruba Central (the title of HPE's page; the page also names 'HPE Networking CX Switches' and 'HPE Aruba Networking Access Points'). HPE says it can be deployed cloud-delivered, on-prem, as-a-service or as a virtual private cloud, with a GreenLake copilot interface.
Juniper switches: Juniper Mist Wired Assurance: Juniper switches are configured in the cloud through the Mist portal: the Juniper Mist Wired Assurance Configuration Guide (21-Oct-26) says it helps configure Juniper switches through the Mist portal, powered by the Juniper Mist Wired Assurance cloud service. The documentation now lives on the 'HPE Juniper Networking' site (networkingdocs.hpe.com), where juniper.net redirects.
Arista switches: CloudVision: CloudVision is Arista's multi-domain management platform (data center, campus, WAN and multicloud), offered as a cloud service (SaaS) or an on-prem appliance (virtual or physical) with the same feature set. Its central API gateway uses OpenConfig, gRPC and REST.
Huawei switches: iMaster NCE-Campus: iMaster NCE-Campus is Huawei's management and control system for campus networks (the specifications text also calls it CloudCampus @ iMaster NCE-Campus): plug-and-play provisioning in four modes, automated VXLAN deployment, multi-tenant management, and 170+ northbound RESTful APIs.
MikroTik: no cloud controller found; CMR, The Dude and REST API: In the pages read, MikroTik has no cloud controller for switches. The fleet tool is CMR: one RouterOS device with the cmr package runs the server and the others connect as clients, with fleet upgrades, alerts and VLAN provisioning on access or trunk ports. The Dude is discontinued and classified as legacy. For automation there is the REST API (HTTPS, under /rest, since RouterOS v7.1beta4).

slides.title: Pre-course assessment (1/2): Ethernet, switching, STP and addressing
notes:
Run the assessment at the start of the day, ungraded and anonymous: the goal is to measure the class starting point, not to pass or fail anyone. Give about ten minutes for the eight questions (this is the first half) and collect the answers on paper or in a poll. The same eight questions return at the end of the module, and the comparison shows what the class learned. Tip: do not correct yet; note which questions most people missed and revisit those points when the topic comes up, for example STP and addressing.

Answer key:
1. B: RFC 894 sets 1500 octets as the maximum IP datagram over Ethernet; 46 octets is the minimum of the data field, padded if needed.
2. B: Frames to an unknown destination MAC are flooded like broadcasts, and the source MAC is associated with the port it arrived on (RFC 4762, 4.1 and 4.2).
3. D: The highest priority (lowest numerical value) wins the root election; on a tie, the lowest MAC address wins (C3 guide, 6-17).
4. C: RFC 1918 reserves 10/8, 172.16/12 (172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255) and 192.168/16; 172.32.0.1 is outside them.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), p. 6-17 (PDF p. 251), set spantree priority, Usage (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] RFC 894, A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over Ethernet Networks (STD 41), Frame Format. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc894.txt
[3] RFC 4762, Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Using LDP Signaling, 4.1 Flooding and Forwarding; 4.2 Address Learning. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4762.txt
[4] RFC 1918, Address Allocation for Private Internets (BCP 5), 3. Private Address Space. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918.txt

slides.title: Pre-course assessment (2/2): addressing, routing and management
notes:
This is the second half of the pre-course assessment: IP addressing, routing and remote management. Stress that these are day-to-day questions for anyone who runs a network, such as picking the right route and knowing why SSH replaced unencrypted access. Record the misses in a simple spreadsheet to compare with the final assessment. Tip: for the routing question, ask someone to draw the table on the board; seeing the most specific route win is worth more than the explanation.

Answer key:
5. C: A /24 spans 256 addresses (RFC 4632, 3.1) and a host number of all zeros or all ones is not allowed (RFC 1122, 3.2.1.3): that leaves 254.
6. C: The router uses the most specific matching route (the longest prefix): 10.1.10.0/24, via R3 (RFC 1812, 2.2.5.2 and 5.2.4.3).
7. B: The packet must be discarded and, unless the destination is multicast, the router must send ICMP Time Exceeded, code 0, to the source (RFC 1812, 5.3.1); the type is 11 (RFC 792).
8. A: RFC 4253 describes the SSH transport layer with strong encryption, host (server) authentication and integrity protection; RFC 4251 summarizes the same.

Sources:
[1] RFC 4632, Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR) (BCP 122), 3.1 Basic Concept and Prefix Notation. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632.txt
[2] RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers (STD 3), 3.2.1.3 Addressing. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122.txt
[3] RFC 1812, Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, 2.2.5.2 CIDR; 5.2.4.3 Next Hop Address (Longest Match); 5.3.1 Time to Live. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812.txt
[4] RFC 792, Internet Control Message Protocol (STD 5), Time Exceeded Message. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc792.txt
[5] RFC 4253, The Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Protocol, 1. Introduction. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4253.txt
[6] RFC 4251, The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Architecture, Abstract. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4251.txt

slides.title: Accessing the switch
notes:
The serial console is the last-resort access and the first access to a new device: VT100 emulator at 9600 bps, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit. On SecureStack the console is DB9 and uses a DB9 female to DB9 female serial cable (part SSCON-CAB). Today the same role is played by Tera Term, PuTTY or OpenSSH with a USB-to-serial adapter. Tip: if the screen shows the boot but does not answer commands, try other flow-control settings in the emulator; the documented console default is flow control disabled. The exact cable wiring is not in the configuration guides, see the Installation Guide for the model.

[1] Extreme Networks Community FAQ: How to set up a Serial Console Session for the SecureStack, "The SecureStacks have a DB9 console port"; DB9 female to DB9 female cable; SSCON-CAB; VT100, 9600/8/1/none. https://community.extremenetworks.com/t5/faqs/how-to-set-up-a-serial-console-session-for-the-securestack/m-p/49445

slides.title: Accessing the switch
notes:
On DFE modules the console is an RJ-45 port that needs an RJ-45 to DB-9 adapter (or USB-serial) and an 8-conductor straight-through RJ-45 cable. The parameters stay at 9600, 8, N, 1 with VT100 emulation. In operations, keep a console adapter in the maintenance kit, because the console is the only access when the network is down. Tip: a console server avoids trips to the rack.

slides.title: Accessing the switch
notes:
Network access: Telnet sends everything in clear text and should be disabled in production; SSH encrypts the session. In the 2007 guides SSH is disabled by default (enable it with set ssh enable) and Telnet is enabled. NetSight, today ExtremeCloud IQ Site Engine, manages devices over SNMP: v1 and v2c send the community in clear text, and only SNMPv3 offers encryption, and only when the security level includes privacy (authPriv). Tip: in the lab, show a Telnet capture and an SSH capture side by side to make the difference visible.

slides.title: Accessing the switch
notes:
The privilege level is set per user: su (super-user), rw (read-write) and ro (read-only), and it shows in the prompt, for example C3(su)->. The question mark builds any command: contextual help replaces memorizing syntax. The set length command adjusts the number of lines per screen (values 5 to 512) and set length 0 disables paging, useful to capture long outputs in a log. Tip: the set length value is written to NV-RAM, so tell others when you change it on shared devices.

slides.title: Access privileges
notes:
The three default users are admin (super-user), rw (read-write) and ro (read-only), all with a blank password. The admin account cannot be deleted or disabled, so the first action is to set a password for it. The rw and ro users should be disabled during initial configuration, because they are well-known accounts to anyone who has seen an Enterasys device. Tip: create named accounts and then disable the default ones; confirm the result with show system login.

slides.title: User management
notes:
Three commands cover the life cycle of an account: set system login creates or changes (with super-user, read-write or read-only privilege and enable or disable state), clear system login removes, and set password changes the password. Read-write and read-only users change only their own password, while the super-user changes any account. The SecureStack C3 accepts up to 16 local accounts. Tip: the user name may be up to 80 characters, but 16 is recommended for correct display in show system login.

slides.title: Working with the CLI
notes:
Manage sessions: set logout defines, in minutes, the idle time before the session closes and show logout displays the current value. The 2007 guides state 15 minutes as the default in the exit command, but the Logout field of show system on SecureStack reports 5 minutes; confirm the real value with show logout. show users lists the console and Telnet sessions, disconnect closes one of them by IP or the console, and tell, which sends a message to other users, exists only on the DFE. Tip: drop forgotten sessions before a maintenance to avoid concurrent changes.

Command history works through a buffer: the history command lists the contents, show history only displays the buffer size (20 lines by default) and set history size [default] changes that size from 1 to 100 lines, being persistent when used with default. cls clears the session screen and exit or quit ends the CLI session. slides.title: Clock
notes:
A correct clock is a prerequisite for logs, certificates and event correlation. show time displays the current time, set time accepts the date (mm/dd/yyyy) and the time (hh:mm:ss, 24-hour) together or separately, and set summertime enables daylight saving with a zone name. 2026 update: Brazil ended daylight saving time in 2019, so summertime should stay disabled on devices in Brazil; in production, prefer synchronizing the clock via NTP/SNTP (SNTP is disabled by default in the 2007 guides). Tip: set the clock before collecting logs of a failure.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), show time and set time (p. 3-16, PDF p. 76); show summertime, set summertime, clear summertime (pp. 3-17 to 3-19, PDF pp. 77-79); Table 1-1 SNTP Disabled (p. 1-4, PDF p. 38) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Prompt, name, banner and IP connectivity
notes:
Define the identity and reachability of the device: set prompt changes the CLI prompt, set system name defines the name (in quotes; blank clears it), set banner motd writes the login message (\n is a new line and \t equals 8 spaces) and clear banner motd removes it. set ip address defines the management IP, with optional mask and gateway: without a mask it assumes the natural mask. The ping options -s and count exist only on the DFE; on SecureStack the syntax is ping host. Tip: use the banner for a legal notice of authorized access and the prompt to identify the device and avoid typing commands on the wrong switch.

slides.title: Clearing the configuration
notes:
In general, clear undoes what was done with set, and the clear config family returns the device to factory defaults. On the DFE, running clear config resets the module to factory configuration; the SecureStack guides do not state that the command reboots the switch. The command that applies a configuration file is configure, and without the append option it replaces the current configuration and requires an automatic reset. Tip: save the configuration to a file (show config outfile) before clearing any device.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), clear config: "resets that module back to its factory defaults" (p. 2-156, PDF p. 182); configure filename [append] (p. 2-137, PDF p. 163) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), clear config (p. 3-70, PDF p. 130); configure filename [append]: replaced configuration requires an automated reset (p. 3-49, PDF p. 109) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Clearing the configuration
notes:
On SecureStack, clear config clears the configuration but preserves the stack numbering, the IP and the licenses; clear config all also resets the stack IDs and priorities, but still does not erase the IP or the advanced feature license. To remove the IP use clear ip address and, to remove a license, clear license. In operations, this avoids having to renumber an entire stack just to clear the configuration. Tip: after clear config all, check show switch, because the unit IDs go back to their defaults.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Considerations About Using Clear Config in a Stack (p. 2-5, PDF p. 51); clear config (p. 3-70, PDF p. 130); license commands do not affect licenses (p. 3-29, PDF p. 89); clear license (p. 3-32, PDF p. 92) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] SecureStack B3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034314-03 (June 2007), Same text in Considerations About Using Clear Config in a Stack (p. 2-5, PDF p. 43); same in A2 (PDF p. 41) and C2 (PDF p. 47) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Clearing the configuration
notes:
On the DFE, the syntax is clear config {mod-num | all}: all clears every module and mod-num clears the given module, which returns to factory defaults. According to the 2007 guides (DFE 5.41 and the 2006 N7 User's Guide), these commands do not affect the IP address; the IP is removed with clear ip address. Optional licenses are removed with clear license. Tip: when clearing a single module in an active chassis, it inherits the system settings from the others, so verify the result with show config.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), clear config mod-num | all, NOTE: "This command will not affect the IP address" (p. 2-156, PDF p. 182); clear ip address (p. 2-46, PDF p. 72); clear license (p. 2-94, PDF p. 120) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE Series and N-SA User's Guide, P/N 9033939-02 (February 2006), clear config mod-num | all, "This command does not affect the switch IP address" (p. 2-13, PDF p. 31) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Rebooting the switch
notes:
On SecureStack, reset with no parameter reboots the entire stack and reset with the unit ID reboots only that member; the configuration is preserved. The device asks for confirmation before reloading. In operations, picking the right member avoids taking the whole stack down. Tip: in automatic persistence mode the configuration is saved every 2 minutes on a standalone switch and every 30 minutes on a stack, so run save config before a reset after a recent change.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), reset [unit] (p. 3-69, PDF p. 129); Configuration Persistence Mode and save config (pp. 3-44 and 3-46, PDF pp. 104 and 106) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Rebooting the switch
notes:
On the DFE, reset reboots the system without losing the configuration and asks for confirmation. reset in hh:mm schedules a reboot after an interval and reset at hh:mm [mm/dd] schedules it for a given time, both with an optional reason. show reset displays the schedule and reset cancel cancels it. Tip: scheduling with reset at, together with set boot system, lets you apply new firmware in the maintenance window without being present at the exact minute.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Section 2.2.12: show reset (p. 2-151, PDF p. 177); reset and reset cancel (p. 2-152, PDF p. 178); reset at (p. 2-154, PDF p. 180); reset in (p. 2-155, PDF p. 181) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Recovering access when passwords are lost
notes:
Historical procedure for SecureStack with local authentication. If RADIUS is in use, first isolate the RADIUS server from the network, because the server passwords override the local ones. Hold the reset button for 5 seconds; the switch logs "Password Reset button has been pressed" on the console and in the log, and the admin, rw and ro passwords return to the blank value. The button sits to the right of the "stack down" connector on the rear (on the A2, to the right of the console port, on the front). Caution: older-hardware C2 units (C2G124-48 and 48P, revision 0B or lower) use a different procedure, which requires the reset during boot.

Sources:
[1] Extreme Networks Community FAQ (Article ID 5476): Password Recovery for the SecureStack Series, Procedure for newer hardware; button location; "Password Reset button has been pressed"; admin, rw and ro reset; RADIUS note; older C2 hardware procedure. https://community.extremenetworks.com/t5/faqs/password-recovery-for-the-securestack-series/m-p/47472

slides.title: Recovering access when passwords are lost
notes:
Historical procedure for DFE modules: remove all modules from the chassis backplane, use anti-static protection, pick one module and toggle switch 8 of the DIP switch bank, reinsert it and wait for the full boot (it becomes the Management Master), then confirm that the admin password went back to the default. Reconnect the other modules afterwards. Only the admin password is recovered this way: the rw and ro passwords cannot be reset externally, so set them again using admin. Tip: show system hardware displays the DIP switch positions.

Sources:
[1] Extreme Networks Community FAQ (Article ID 5022): S/N/K-Series Reset of the Admin Password, Procedure: pull all blades, anti-static precautions, toggle DIP switch 8, reinsert and boot; rw and ro cannot be reset externally. https://community.extremenetworks.com/t5/faqs/s-n-k-series-reset-of-the-admin-password/m-p/46271
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), set password: "The admin password can be reset by toggling dip switch 8" (p. 2-29, PDF p. 55); show system hardware, Dip Switch Bank (p. 2-53, PDF p. 79) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Password recovery
notes:
Extreme Switch Engine: Extreme Switch Engine 33.7.1 (recommended 33.7.1.6-Patch1-32) on universal hardware 5320/5420/5520/5720; maintenance 32.7.4.15-Patch1-14

Note: Console required. 'With default configuration' boots factory defaults and deletes no files or licenses: primary.cfg is lost only if you save before reloading it. [2][3][5]

Source of each line:
1. Attach a terminal to the console port and restart the switch (no login needed; recovery is local only). Hold the space bar until the Boot Menu shows (30 s window).: [1][2]
2. In the Boot Menu, use the arrow keys and Enter to pick 'EXOS: Primary ... with default configuration'. Do not pick 'EXOS: Rescue'. Files and licenses are not deleted.: [1][2][5]
3. Log in as admin with an empty password. The old primary.cfg is still on flash: check with ls and do NOT save now, because saving overwrites it with the blank configuration.: [3]
4. To keep the configuration, create the autoexec.xsf script with vi; it creates a temporary admin account.: [3][4]
5. Select the old configuration file and reboot WITHOUT saving (answer n to the prompt); the script runs at boot.: [3][4]
6. Log in with the temporary account. An account password cannot be read: delete and re-create the account whose password was lost.: [3][4]
7. Log in with the re-created account, delete the temporary account and the script, then save. To avoid losing access again, configure a failsafe account.: [3][4][6]

slides.title: Password recovery
notes:
Extreme Fabric Engine: Extreme 5520-48T (universal hardware) running Fabric Engine 9.4.1.0 (v9.4 documentation)

Note: Needs console access and a GTAC privilege password. Option 7 resets only the CLI passwords (6 and 8 restore factory defaults). With an rwa session 'cli password' is enough. After reset: rwa/rwa. [4][6]

Source of each line:
1. Connect to the serial console (115200, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, no parity, no flow control). On Universal platforms you may need to press the spacebar to get a console response.: [1][4]
2. Power the switch off for a full 60 seconds, then boot it, to avoid the 'Invalid Password! Try Again.' message.: [4]
3. During boot, right after the line 'VSP Linux Uncompressing /boot/a/appfs.tgz ...' (the line for the Universal 5520), type 123! and press Enter.: [4][5]
4. In the 'Lifecycle recovery menu' choose option 7, Reset all CLI local login passwords (options 6 and 8 go to factory defaults).: [4]
5. The menu shows Release#, Serial# and the time. Send them to GTAC and request the privilege password.: [4]
6. Enter the privilege password, then leave the menu with q.: [4]
7. Log in with rwa/rwa (admin/admin when enhanced-security mode is on) and change the password right away.: [4][2][3][6]

slides.title: File management on the switch
notes:
Three purposes for the internal file system: configuration backup, storing configuration versions and managing firmware files. On SecureStack the configuration is saved automatically to NVRAM in "auto" mode; in manual mode you must use save config. Tip: before any change window, generate a file with show config outfile and copy it to an external server; never leave the only copy on the switch itself.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Configuration Persistence Mode (p. 3-44, PDF p. 104); dir (p. 3-46, PDF p. 106); show config outfile (p. 3-48, PDF p. 108) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Managing Configuration and Image Files: dir, show config, configure, copy (pp. 2-131 to 2-140, PDF pp. 157-166) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: File management on the switch
notes:
dir lists firmware images and user files (configurations, logs), show file displays the content of a text file and delete removes a file. The valid directories for delete are /images and /configs on SecureStack and /images and /slotN on the DFE. Tip: use dir before and after any copy to confirm the file size and, for images, the (Active) and (Boot) flags.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), dir (p. 3-46, PDF p. 106) and example (p. 3-47, PDF p. 107); show file (p. 3-47); delete (p. 3-50, PDF p. 110) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: File management
notes:
The copy source destination command moves files between the local file system and remote servers. The source or destination can be a local path (/images and /configs on SecureStack, /images and /slotN on the DFE) or a URL. TFTP works on both platforms, but the FTP URL with credentials appears only in the DFE guide. Tip: use FTP, which the DFE guide describes as the most robust transfer mechanism, and remember that TFTP protects neither credentials nor content.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), copy: "a local file path in the configs directory, or the URL of a TFTP server" (p. 3-50, PDF p. 110); delete: valid directories /images and /configs (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), copy: "valid directories are /images and /slotN, or the URL of an FTP or TFTP server" (p. 2-138, PDF p. 164); FTP is "the most robust downloading mechanism" (p. 2-116, PDF p. 142) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[3] SecureStack B3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034314-03 (June 2007), No FTP URL in the SecureStack guides A2, B2, B3, C2 and C3 (only tftp:// appears) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: File management
notes:
Real examples from the DFE guide: show config outfile writes the active configuration to a file; copy tftp:// or ftp:// (anonymous or with user and password) brings the firmware into the file system under a chosen name; copy between slotN and a server URL backs up and restores configurations; copy slot3/myconfig slot5/myconfig duplicates between slots. The destination module of a configuration file must have the same hardware configuration as the source module. Tip: name files with date and device to make restores easier.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), copy and examples (pp. 2-138 to 2-139, PDF pp. 164-165); show config [all] [facility] [outfile outfile] (p. 2-135, PDF p. 161) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: File management
notes:
SecureStack examples: show config outfile configs/name writes the active configuration to a file; copy tftp://server/file system:image downloads a firmware image; copy tftp://server/file configs/file brings a configuration from the server to the switch (this is the guide example); and dir lists the images and the configuration and log files of the switch. To use a downloaded configuration, the command configure configs/file executes it and, without the append option, replaces the current configuration and requires an automatic chassis reset; delete removes a file from /images or /configs. Tip: copy accepts a local path in configs or a TFTP URL as the source, so for a backup in the opposite direction swap source and destination: copy configs/file tftp://server/file.

[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), dir [filename] and Example (p. 3-46 and 3-47, PDF pp. 106-107); show config [all | facility] [outfile {configs/filename}] (p. 3-48, PDF p. 108); configure filename [append] and its example (p. 3-49, PDF p. 109); copy source destination and its two examples, delete filename (p. 3-50, PDF p. 110) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Reconfiguring the switch from files
notes:
configure filename [append] executes a configuration file stored on the switch. Without append, the current configuration is replaced entirely by the file and the device reboots automatically (after asking for confirmation); with append, the effect is the same as pasting the file text into the CLI, useful for incremental adjustments. In operations, append lets you apply a small configuration fragment without taking the switch down. Tip: use append for fragments and the full mode only to restore a backup.

slides.title: Files and configuration backups (1/2)
notes:
Side-by-side view of block B05. The full commands and the source of every line are on the vendor slides that follow.

• No RFC exists for SFTP or SCP. SFTP is only the expired draft-ietf-secsh-filexfer-13 (2006); since OpenSSH 9.0 (2022-04-08) scp uses the SFTP protocol by default instead of legacy scp/rcp.
• TFTP (RFC 1350, STD 33) uses UDP port 69 and has no user authentication, so use it only on an isolated management network.
• NETCONF (RFC 6241) standardises the candidate datastore, discard-changes and confirmed-commit (with confirm-timeout); it runs over SSH on TCP port 830 (RFC 6242).

slides.title: Files and configuration backups (2/2)
notes:
Side-by-side view of block B05. The full commands and the source of every line are on the vendor slides that follow.

• No RFC exists for SFTP or SCP. SFTP is only the expired draft-ietf-secsh-filexfer-13 (2006); since OpenSSH 9.0 (2022-04-08) scp uses the SFTP protocol by default instead of legacy scp/rcp.
• TFTP (RFC 1350, STD 33) uses UDP port 69 and has no user authentication, so use it only on an isolated management network.
• NETCONF (RFC 6241) standardises the candidate datastore, discard-changes and confirmed-commit (with confirm-timeout); it runs over SSH on TCP port 830 (RFC 6242).

slides.title: Firmware upgrade
notes:
Upgrade procedure on SecureStack: the switch stores two images (the active one and a backup), so check the space with dir and delete an old image if needed; test the ping to the TFTP server and confirm the server root directory; copy the image with copy tftp://server/file system:image (system:image is a keyword, not a file name); select the image for the next boot with set boot system and reboot. Confirm with dir the name under which the image was stored and with show boot system which image will be loaded. Tip: keep the previous image as a backup to roll back if the new firmware fails.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Downloading a New Firmware Image: TFTP and dual images (p. 3-37, PDF p. 97); copy ... system:image (p. 3-50, PDF p. 110); dir example with two images (p. 3-47, PDF p. 107); show boot system and set boot system (pp. 3-40 to 3-41, PDF pp. 100-101) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] SecureStack B3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034314-03 (June 2007), Same copy example (p. 3-50); same in A2, B2 and C2 (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Firmware upgrade
notes:
Procedure on the DFE: check the free flash space (show system hardware shows the free space of /flash0 and /flash1), delete an old image if space is short, test the ping and the server directory, and copy the image giving it a name (copy tftp://server/file name). The DFE accepts FTP, described in the guide as the most robust mechanism, besides TFTP. Then set boot system name selects the image; the command asks whether to reset the system right away. Images are mirrored automatically to all compatible modules in the chassis. Tip: use dir to check (Active) and (Boot) before and after the reset.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Downloading a New Firmware Image: multiple images stored (p. 2-116, PDF p. 142); copy (p. 2-138, PDF p. 164); set boot system (p. 2-121, PDF p. 147); dir Table 2-8, Location mirroring (p. 2-132, PDF p. 158); show system hardware, free space (p. 2-53, PDF p. 79) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

notes:

slides.title: Lab: Basic Maintenance
notes:
Basic maintenance lab, covering the protection cycle of a configuration: save it to a file, clear to factory defaults, restore with configure, copy to the TFTP server, rename and view the file on the server, bring it back, run the password recovery and upgrade the firmware. Ask participants to note the command order. Tip: do the password recovery and the firmware upgrade last, since both require physical access or a reboot.

Rule from the original 2007 program: after each lab, save the configuration named after the lab and the bench number.

slides.title: Physical Interface Naming
notes:
Every port is named as type.slot.port, for example ge.1.1; the type indicates the interface (fe, ge, tg) or a virtual system port (vlan, lag, host, rtr, lpbk). The list on the slide is the Matrix N one: the DFE guide also lists com (console), lo (software loopback) and bp (backplane ports of the FTM-1 modules), while SecureStack uses only fe, ge, tg, host, vlan and lag. The name is used in almost every command (show port, set vlan egress, set port speed), so ask students to memorize it right away. The type describes the interface and not what was negotiated: in the guide example, port ge.3.14 shows a speed of 10 Mbps. Note: the loopback type is lpbk; the lbpk spelling of the original version was corrected.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Port String Syntax Used in the CLI (p. 4-2, PDF p. 262) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Physical Interface Naming
notes:
On the Matrix N the slot field is the chassis slot number, counted from left to right; on the N7 it goes from 1 to 7. On SecureStack the field is the unit number (device number) in the stack, from 1 to 8 on the C3. By default the IDs are assigned on a first-come, first-served basis, so powering on the units one by one, from top to bottom, gives sequential numbering; once assigned, the ID is saved and persists across reboots. Slot 0 identifies the virtual system ports (lag, vlan, host and loopback), as in lag.0.1 and host.0.1. Tip: check the numbering with show switch before configuring the ports of a new stack.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Port String Syntax Used in the CLI, slot location (p. 4-2, PDF p. 262) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Stack unit IDs, first-come first-served and power on from top to bottom (p. 2-2, PDF p. 48); unit number 1 to 8 (p. 4-1, PDF p. 135); show switch (p. 2-7) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[3] SecureStack A2 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 2.00.xx, P/N 9034155-07 (August 2007), Same power-on rule (p. 2-2, PDF p. 38); same in B2, B3 and C2 (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Physical Interface Naming
notes:
The port number identifies the physical port on each module or stack member, and the count restarts for each interface type. That is why ge.1.1 is the first Gigabit port of slot 1 even if 24 Fast Ethernet ports come before it; if the uplink is of the same type as the front panel, the numbering continues (fe.1.49 after fe.1.48). This happens, for example, on expansion modules (NEM) with Gigabit uplinks on Fast Ethernet cards. Tip: use show port status to see the real list of ports and types before building a port-string.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Port number: numbering per port type, 48 FE + 6 Mini-GBIC example (p. 4-2, PDF p. 262) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Physical Interface Naming
notes:
The port-string accepts wildcards (*) and lists: fe.*.* is all 100 Mbps ports in the chassis, ge.2.* is all Gigabit ports of slot or unit 2 and *.*.* is all ports of any type. Ranges use a hyphen and lists use a comma, as in fe.1.1,fe.1.3,fe.1.7-10. The DFE guide shows ranges only in the port field; the slot-range form, such as ge.1-7.10, appears in the SecureStack examples (ge.3-5.*), so validate it with a show on the Matrix N before using it. Tip: before any set or clear, run the same port-string with show port status; *.*.* also reaches the uplinks and can cut off management access.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Port String Syntax Used in the CLI, Examples: wildcards, ranges and lists (pp. 4-3 and 4-4, PDF pp. 263-264) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Checking the operational state of ports
notes:
Three commands cover basic port diagnostics: show port shows whether the port is enabled for switching, show port status shows the operational and administrative state, speed, duplex and type, and show port counters shows the traffic and error counters. The switch or mib2 option of counters separates the switch statistics from the MIB-II interface statistics. A port that accumulates errors must have its cause investigated (the port lab slide shows a case with different duplex on the two sides). Tip: note the counters, generate traffic and look again, comparing the change instead of the absolute value.

[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), show port (p. 4-25, PDF p. 285); show port status (p. 4-26, PDF p. 286); show port counters (p. 4-28, PDF p. 288) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Managing port parameters
notes:
To administratively disable or enable a port use set port disable and set port enable. When disabled, the switch drops the physical link and stops learning MAC addresses on that port. The alias gives the port a readable name (for example the user or the link) and is shown in show port status; if the name is omitted, the alias is cleared. Tip: standardize the aliases (destination and purpose) at installation time, because the alias is the first information the operator reads during an incident.

slides.title: Managing port configuration
notes:
The golden rule is that both ends of a link must agree: either both with auto-negotiation enabled, or both configured manually with negotiation disabled. If only one side negotiates, it cannot discover the duplex of the other and the usual result is a duplex mismatch, with the link up but FCS and alignment errors on one side, runts on the other and very poor performance. When the other side cannot be changed, leave auto-negotiation on and limit what the port advertises (advertised ability). Remember that set port speed and set port duplex only take effect with negotiation disabled, and that the default without negotiation is 10 Mbps half duplex. Also beware of auto-MDI/MDIX, covered on its own slide.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Setting Auto-Negotiation and Advertised Ability (p. 4-14, PDF p. 148); set port speed takes effect only with auto-negotiation disabled (p. 4-10, PDF p. 144); default speed 10 Mbps and half duplex (Table 1-1, p. 1-3, PDF p. 37) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Setting Auto-Negotiation and Advertised Ability (p. 4-51, PDF p. 311); default speed and duplex (Table 2-1, p. 2-4, PDF p. 30) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[3] Cisco: Configuring and Troubleshooting Ethernet 10/100/1000Mb Half/Full Duplex Auto-Negotiation, Sections "When to Use Ethernet 10/100 Mb Auto-Negotiation" and "Auto-Negotiation on Catalyst Switches that Run Cisco IOS Software" (duplex mismatch, FCS/alignment errors and runts). https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/lan-switching/ethernet/10561-3.html

slides.title: Auto-negotiation on ports
notes:
This slide groups the auto-negotiation commands: show port negotiation and set port negotiation turn the feature on and off, and show port advertise lists, per port, three columns: the capability, what is advertised and what the partner advertised (remote). With set port advertise and clear port advertise you add or remove modes (10t, 10tfd, 100tx, 100txfd, 1000t, 1000tfd, pause) from the negotiation, which lets you, for example, make a partner that cannot be configured settle on 100 Mbps full. The syntax shown is the SecureStack one; on the Matrix N set port advertise accepts the same list plus 1000x and 1000xfd (fiber), and apause, spause and bpause. Tip: after changing the advertise, unplug and replug the cable to force a new negotiation.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), show port negotiation / set port negotiation (pp. 4-14 and 4-15, PDF pp. 148-149); show port advertise with capability, advertised and remote columns (pp. 4-15 and 4-16, PDF pp. 149-150); set port advertise {port-string}{10t | 10tfd | 100tx | 100txfd | 1000t | 1000tfd | pause} (p. 4-16, PDF p. 150); clear port advertise (p. 4-17, PDF p. 151) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), set port advertise with 1000x, 1000xfd, apause, spause and bpause (p. 4-59, PDF p. 319); show port negotiation (p. 4-52, PDF p. 312) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Port speed and duplex configuration
notes:
To fix speed and duplex use set port speed (10, 100 or 1000) and set port duplex (full or half), and check them with show port speed and show port duplex. These commands set the default speed and duplex of the port and only take effect on ports with auto-negotiation disabled, which is why the slide insists on this point. If negotiation is turned off without adjusting the values, the port falls back to the factory default, 10 Mbps half duplex (except fiber, which assumes full duplex at its nominal speed). Tip: when fixing a port manually, configure the other end of the link with the same values and check with show port status on both ends.

slides.title: Flow control
notes:
IEEE 802.3x flow control prevents an interface from being overwhelmed: the congested receiver sends a PAUSE frame (Annex 31B of 802.3, multicast address 01-80-C2-00-00-01) asking the sender to suspend transmission. On SecureStack the feature is global (show flowcontrol and set flowcontrol); on the Matrix N it is per port, with show port flowcontrol, which shows the pause counts sent and received, and set port flowcontrol using the receive, send or both options, and the pause capability is also advertised in auto-negotiation. 2026 update: 802.3x-1997 is now part of IEEE 802.3 (Annex 31B; current edition 802.3-2022), and IEEE 802.1Qbb (Priority-based Flow Control, approved in 2011) allows flow control per traffic class on full-duplex links. Tip: if on the Matrix N the pause counters of a port keep growing, investigate the slow receiver before blaming the link.

slides.title: Broadcast suppression
notes:
Broadcast suppression limits, in packets per second, the broadcasts received on each port, and protects against broadcast storms and ARP sweeps; multicast traffic is not affected. On SecureStack the default is 14881 pps on all ports, regardless of speed (it equals the maximum rate of 64-byte frames at 10 Mbps, by calculation); on the Matrix N the default is no limit. The maximum value is 148810 pps on Fast Ethernet and 1488100 pps on Gigabit, and on the Matrix N setting the maximum disables thresholding. Limiting too much can disturb legitimate ARP and DHCP; the ideal is to find the source of the excess and fix the network design. Tip: show port broadcast shows the broadcast total and the threshold of each port.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Configuring Broadcast Suppression, default 14881 pps, multicast not affected (p. 4-29, PDF p. 163); set/clear port broadcast, maximum 148810 (FE) and 1488100 (GE) (p. 4-30, PDF p. 164); Table 1-1 (p. 1-3, PDF p. 37) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Port broadcast suppression default "Disabled (no broadcast limit)" (Table 2-1, p. 2-4, PDF p. 30); set port broadcast, maximum disables thresholding (p. 4-86, PDF p. 346); clear port broadcast (p. 4-87, PDF p. 347) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Auto-MDI/MDIX
notes:
Auto-MDI/MDIX detects whether the cable is straight-through (MDI) or crossover (MDIX) and adapts, removing the need for crossover cables between switches or hubs. On the Matrix N, show port mdix shows the mode, set port mdix forces auto, mdi or mdix, and clear port mdix returns to the default auto; the SecureStack guides have no MDI/MDIX configuration command. The risk is operational: connecting two ports of the same switch with a cable brings the link up on both ends, and without Spanning Tree the result is a broadcast loop that takes the segment down, exactly the scenario of the broadcast suppression lab. Tip: before any test with a cable between ports of the same switch, confirm that Spanning Tree is enabled and know which cable to remove.

slides.title: Protected Ports
notes:
Protected ports prevent ports of the same group from exchanging traffic with each other, even in the same VLAN. A protected port can still talk to unprotected ports (the default for all ports) and to protected ports of another group, provided they are in the same VLAN; a port can belong to only one group. The guide limits the function to the ports of a single switch, with no effect across switches in the network (for a stack, validate on the equipment), and it is exclusive to SecureStack: the Matrix N guides do not have the command. A typical case is isolating users of the same VLAN from each other while keeping access to the uplink, which must stay unprotected. Tip: validate the result with a ping between the ports and check show port protected.

[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Configuring Protected Ports, operation and limits (p. 4-51, PDF p. 185) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Protected Ports
notes:
The protected port commands follow the set, show and clear pattern: set port protected port-string group-id places the ports in a group (group-id goes from 0 to 2, that is, up to three groups), show port protected queries by port or by group, and clear port protected removes the protection. Each group can be given a name of up to 32 characters with set port protected name, which helps document its purpose. Remember that clear port protected with no parameters unprotects everything. Tip: document the groups with clear names and keep the uplink out of every group.

slides.title: Jumbo Frames
notes:
Jumbo frames allow Gigabit ports to transmit frames larger than standard Ethernet, usually to reduce overhead in large transfers. The guide speaks of up to 10 KB: SecureStack shows 9216 bytes in show port jumbo, and the Matrix N shows an MTU of 10239. The factory default is enabled on SecureStack and disabled on the Matrix N, and clear port jumbo returns the port to the default. Jumbo frames are not part of IEEE 802.3, which defines a 1518-byte basic frame (1522 with an 802.1Q tag and 2000 bytes for the envelope frame of 802.3as-2006), and IP over Ethernet uses 1500 bytes (RFC 894), so every device in the path must support the same size; on the Matrix N keep path MTU discovery enabled. Tip: confirm with show port jumbo on both ends and test with a large-packet ping before going to production.

slides.title: Port Mirroring
notes:
Port mirroring copies the traffic of one or more ports to a monitoring port where a protocol analyzer, an IDS, a voice recorder or a performance tool sits. It is the way to observe a communication in which the analyzer does not take part, without inserting a device in the path. The session only becomes operational when there is a destination port and at least one source; the destination port acts as a mirror only in that condition. Tip: remove the mirror when the capture is finished, because the destination port is dedicated to it while the session is active.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Port Mirroring, mirroring features (p. 4-31, PDF p. 165) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Configuring Port Mirroring (p. 4-88, PDF p. 348) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Port Mirroring
notes:
On SecureStack mirroring is many-to-one: up to 8 source ports mirrored to a single destination port, and there can be only one destination port per stack. Receive and transmit traffic is mirrored, and LAG ports and the physical ports that make them up cannot be mirrored, so only physical ports outside LAGs work as sources. The number 8 appears in the A2, B2 and C2 guides; the C3 and B3 guide text omits the number. The C3 adds remote port mirroring, which carries the mirrored traffic in a dedicated VLAN to another switch, a feature that does not exist on the A2, B2 and C2. Tip: since LAG ports cannot be mirrored, observe the traffic of an aggregated link at another point of the path or temporarily remove the LAG.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack A2 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 2.00.xx, P/N 9034155-07 (August 2007), Mirroring Features: up to 8 source ports, one destination port per stack (p. 5-33, PDF p. 151); same in B2 (p. 4-31) and C2 (p. 4-32) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Mirroring Features (p. 4-31, PDF p. 165); remote port mirroring not supported on A2, B2 or C2 (same page); LAG ports and their underlying physical ports cannot be mirrored (p. 4-34, PDF p. 168) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Port Mirroring
notes:
On the Matrix N mirroring is more flexible: the source can be a physical port (including FTM-1 ports), a virtual port such as a LAG or host, a VLAN or an IDS mirror. Each DFE-Platinum module supports up to 16 mirroring destinations, in any combination of ports, VLANs and IDS (the N-SA supports 64), and any destination can receive several sources. The direction is chosen with rx, tx or both (default both). An IDS mirror accepts an unlimited number of sources but reserves eight destination ports. Tip: mirroring a whole VLAN can generate more traffic than the destination port can carry.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Supported Mirrors (p. 4-88, PDF p. 348); IDS Mirroring Considerations and Active Destination Port Configurations: 16 destinations per DFE-Platinum, 64 on N-SA (p. 4-89, PDF p. 349); set port mirroring [both | rx | tx], default both (p. 4-92, PDF p. 352) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Configuring port mirroring
notes:
show port mirroring displays source, destination, the mirrored direction (Rx and Tx) and whether mirroring is enabled or disabled. To create the mirror use set port mirroring create source destination and then enable; to remove it use clear port mirroring source destination. On the Matrix N the command also accepts rx, tx or both (default both) and the igmp-mcast option to mirror IGMP multicast frames; on SecureStack there is no direction selection. The DFE syntax on the slide reproduces the line of the guide, which combines the two forms of the command. Tip: always check the "enabled" status in show port mirroring and remove the mirror when the capture is finished.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), show port mirroring, set port mirroring, clear port mirroring (pp. 4-33 and 4-34, PDF pp. 167-168) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Link Aggregation LACP
notes:
LACP groups several physical links between two devices into one logical link, the LAG (Link Aggregation Group), represented on the switch by a lag.x.x interface. Two Gigabit links become a 2 Gbps LAG and, if one of them fails, traffic continues over the other: more bandwidth and fault tolerance. The SecureStack C3 offers six aggregators per module (lag.0.1 to lag.0.6) and the Matrix N offers 48 (lag.0.1 to lag.0.48). The combined bandwidth does not mean a single conversation can exceed 1 Gbps, because traffic is distributed among the members by an outport algorithm, whose default is DIP-SIP (destination and source IP addresses). 2026 update: LACP started as IEEE 802.3ad-2000, now superseded, and link aggregation is maintained by the 802.1 group as IEEE 802.1AX, whose current edition is 802.1AX-2020.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP), 802.3ad, enabled by default (p. 4-37, PDF p. 171); LACP Terminology, six aggregators lag.0.1 to lag.0.6 (p. 4-38, PDF p. 172); default outport algorithm DIP-SIP (Table 1-1, p. 1-3, PDF p. 37) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Configuring LACP, 802.3ad (p. 4-95, PDF p. 355); 48 aggregator ports lag.0.1 to lag.0.48 (p. 4-100, PDF p. 360); set lacp outportAlgorithm {dip-sip | da-sa | round-robin} (p. 4-125, PDF p. 385) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[3] IEEE Std 802.1AX-2020, IEEE Standard for Local and Metropolitan Area Networks--Link Aggregation, IEEE SA record: Active Standard, published 2020-05-29, supersedes 802.1AX-2014. https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/802.1AX/6768/
[4] IEEE 802.3ad-2000, Part 3: CSMA/CD Access Method and Physical Layer Specifications - Aggregation of Multiple Link Segments, IEEE SA record: Superseded Standard; link aggregation is now IEEE 802.1AX. https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/802.3ad/1088/

slides.title: Link Aggregation LACP
notes:
The ports of a LAG must operate at the same speed and in full duplex. LACP is enabled by default, so when several cables are connected between two switches with LACP the LAG forms by itself. Mind the VLANs: the LAG and all its ports must be in the egress list of the desired VLAN, because if a dynamic LAG is reduced to one port the switch removes the LAG from the VLAN and adds the remaining port, which may land in the wrong VLAN. If the other side does not speak LACP there is no dynamic aggregation and the switch simply blocks the redundant paths through Spanning Tree; with neither LAG nor Spanning Tree, several links between two switches form a loop. Tip: check with show lacp on both sides, and use set lacp static when the partner does not support LACP.

slides.title: Link Aggregation LACP
notes:
These commands cover LACP at two levels: show lacp and set lacp handle the global state and the aggregators (lag.0.x), while show port lacp and set port lacp handle the physical ports. In show port lacp the status detail or summary and counters options show the protocol state (actor and partner keys and states) and the LACP counters per port. The show lacp state form, which shows only the global state, exists on the Matrix N; on SecureStack show lacp accepts only the port-string of an aggregator. Tip: if a LAG does not form, compare the administrative keys (admin key) and the port state on both sides with show port lacp port ... status detail.

slides.title: 802.1Q VLAN
notes:
A VLAN is a logically isolated layer 2 broadcast domain: ports in different VLANs can only communicate through an L3 router. To extend a VLAN across switches the VLAN ID must be the same on all of them. By default all ports belong to the DEFAULT VLAN, ID 1, untagged, and that VLAN cannot be deleted. The management interface (host port) must be in the VLAN of the IP network where the switch is managed: on SecureStack this is done with set host vlan, and on the Matrix N with the PVID and egress of the host port. The SecureStack C3 guide accepts up to 1024 VLANs with IDs from 1 to 4093, and the Matrix N guide up to 4094 VLANs. 2026 update: the current standard is IEEE 802.1Q-2022, in Active status.

Sources:

slides.title: 802.1Q VLAN
notes:
Three concepts explain VLAN behavior on a port. Egress defines the VLANs in which the port transmits and whether it does so tagged or untagged; a port can have several VLANs in egress. The PVID is the VLAN in which the port classifies frames that arrive untagged. The 802.1Q tag says which VLAN the frame belongs to and, when present, takes precedence over the PVID unless a filter exists: ingress filtering (set port ingress-filter) discards frames whose VLAN is not in the port egress list. Tip: an access port is egress untagged in one VLAN with that VLAN as its PVID; a trunk port is egress tagged for the VLANs it carries.

slides.title: 802.1Q VLAN
notes:
GVRP (GARP VLAN Registration Protocol) creates VLANs dynamically across the network. The VLAN is announced by GARP frames sent to the GVRP multicast address; the switch that receives them creates the VLAN and adds the receiving port to its egress list as tagged, passing the announcement on through the other GVRP ports. Dynamic registrations expire if the station leaves the network, while a manually configured VLAN is static. Even without planning, a GVRP port accepts VLANs from a neighbor, so disable GVRP where it is not needed: on SecureStack it is enabled globally and disabled on the ports, but on the Matrix N it is enabled on all ports. To block a VLAN on a port use egress forbidden. 2026 update: GVRP, based on GARP, was replaced by MVRP (802.1ak), now part of IEEE 802.1Q.

slides.title: Managing VLANs
notes:
These are the basic VLAN commands. show vlan lists the VLANs, static and dynamic, with the egress ports and the untagged ports. set vlan create creates the VLAN (also enable and disable), set vlan name names it, clear vlan removes it and clear vlan name removes the name. VLAN 1 is static and cannot be deleted. The portinfo option of show vlan belongs to SecureStack; on the Matrix N the syntax is show vlan [static] [vlan-list]. Tip: create and name the VLAN before putting ports in it, and use names that describe the function.

slides.title: Managing VLANs
notes:
The PVID of a port is queried with show port vlan, changed with set port vlan and returned to the default (VLAN 1) with clear port vlan. set port vlan only defines the classification of untagged frames: without the matching egress the port does not transmit in the VLAN. That is why the modify-egress option exists, which adds the port as untagged to the PVID VLAN and removes it from the other untagged lists; with no-modify-egress no egress list is changed. Tip: after changing the PVID, confirm with show port egress, and note that the last line of this slide repeats the first.

slides.title: VLAN Egress
notes:
Egress is the list of ports that transmit a VLAN: if the VLAN is not in egress on the port, its traffic does not leave through it. If the egress is tagged the frame leaves with the 802.1Q tag, and if it is untagged it leaves without a tag. A port can have several VLANs in egress, but usually only one untagged. The forbidden egress, covered on the next slide, also prevents the dynamic joining of the port to the VLAN. Tip: on a trunk between switches use the same tagged configuration on both ends; if one end sends the VLAN untagged, the other will classify it by the port PVID.

slides.title: VLAN Egress
notes:
The egress commands: show port egress shows, per port, the VLANs, whether tagged or untagged and the registration type (static or dynamic); set vlan egress adds ports to the VLAN list and clear vlan egress removes them; show vlan vlan-id shows all ports that have egress for the VLAN. Mind the default: if untagged, forbidden or tagged is not specified, the port is added as tagged, which surprises those who expect an access port. clear vlan egress accepts forbidden to also remove the prohibition. Tip: for an access port use set vlan egress vlan-list port untagged, adjust the PVID and take the port out of VLAN 1.

slides.title: Lab: Port configuration
notes:
Port lab, which goes through name, disabling, manual speed and duplex, counters and auto-negotiation advertising. In steps c and d the switch port is set to 100 Full and the PC card to 100 Half: this is a deliberate duplex mismatch, and the counters in step e should show errors (FCS and alignment on one side, runts on the other). In step f go back with set port negotiation enable; in step h leave only 10t advertised on the port by clearing the other modes with clear port advertise, and replug the cable to renegotiate; in step j restore all modes with set port advertise. Since the SecureStack and Matrix N guides do not document a command to zero the counters of a port, step g was rewritten: note the show port counters values in step e and compare the change after generating more traffic.

Rule from the original 2007 program: after each lab, save the configuration named after the lab and the bench number.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Port counters: show port counters (p. 4-5, PDF p. 139); set port advertise and clear port advertise (pp. 4-16 and 4-17, PDF pp. 150-151); set port disable (p. 4-7, PDF p. 141); set port alias (p. 4-8, PDF p. 142) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

[3] Cisco: Configuring and Troubleshooting Ethernet 10/100/1000Mb Half/Full Duplex Auto-Negotiation, Auto-negotiation with a duplex mismatch: rapid increase of FCS and alignment errors on the half-duplex side and runts on the full-duplex port. https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/lan-switching/ethernet/10561-3.html

slides.title: Lab: Link Aggregation
notes:
Aggregation lab: connect two or more cables between the switches and confirm that LACP forms the LAG (show lacp and show port lacp port ... status summary). With a PC on each switch and a continuous ping, unplug one cable: the ping should lose at most a few packets and continue over the other member. Replug and watch the member return to the LAG; when the other cable is removed, the LAG is reduced to one port and, as the guide describes, the switch removes the LAG from the VLAN and adds the remaining port, which is why the LAG and the ports must be in the same VLAN. Tip: ask students to note the state of the physical ports and of the LAG at each step.

Rule from the original 2007 program: after each lab, save the configuration named after the lab and the bench number.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), LACP operation, LAG reduced to one port, VLAN membership (p. 4-39, PDF p. 173); show lacp and show port lacp (pp. 4-40 and 4-46, PDF pp. 174 and 180) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Lab: Port Protect
notes:
Protected ports lab, exclusive to SecureStack. Create two named groups (group-id 0 to 2), with two ports in each, and connect two PCs to ports of the same group: the ping between them must fail even in the same VLAN. When one of the PCs is moved to a port of the other group, the ping should work, because different groups can communicate. Tip: confirm the configuration with show port protected and do not protect the uplink port.

Rule from the original 2007 program: after each lab, save the configuration named after the lab and the bench number.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Configuring Protected Ports (pp. 4-51 to 4-54, PDF pp. 185-188) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Lab: VLAN
notes:
VLAN lab: create the VLANs, extend them between switches with tagged egress on the link between them and compare the behavior of tagged and untagged frames on ports with different PVIDs. For item d, the guide offers ingress filtering (set port ingress-filter), which discards frames whose VLAN is not in the port egress list, and set port discard (tagged, untagged, both or none), which discards all frames with or without a tag. In item e, change the egress and PVID and check with show port egress and show port vlan. In item f, disable GVRP: on SecureStack it is already disabled on the ports, but on the Matrix N it is enabled, and if needed use set gvrp disable with the port-string.

Rule from the original 2007 program: after each lab, save the configuration named after the lab and the bench number.

slides.title: Lab: Broadcast Suppression
notes:
Broadcast suppression lab, which reproduces a loop on purpose. With a ping running between the PC and the switch, connect two switch ports to each other (step b) and watch the CPU with show system utilization cpu. Mirror one of the ports to the PC port and capture the traffic to see that it is looping broadcasts; if mirroring is not possible, first disconnect the cable of step b and reconnect it afterwards (steps d and e). If the traffic is broadcast, configure broadcast suppression with set port broadcast and finish by disconnecting the two ports. Note: with Spanning Tree enabled one of the ports may be blocked, which changes the result; decide with the students whether it stays on.

Rule from the original 2007 program: after each lab, save the configuration named after the lab and the bench number.

slides.title: Spanning Tree Protocol
notes:
The original 802.1d (STP) was removed from the IEEE specification when the 802.1D-2004 revision incorporated RSTP (802.1w) and dropped the STP of Clause 8. On SecureStack and the Matrix N the default Spanning Tree version is MSTP (802.1s), which interoperates with RSTP and with 802.1d, and set spantree version lets you choose mstp, rstp or stpcompatible. A bridge in stpcompatible mode only transmits 802.1d BPDUs and prevents the rapid transition of non-edge ports, which is why the guide recommends keeping the default. 2026 update: 802.1D-2004 itself was incorporated into IEEE 802.1Q, and the active edition is 802.1Q-2022, which carries RSTP and MSTP. Tip: an old 802.1d switch in the network forces the neighboring bridges to use 802.1d rules on that connection.

slides.title: IEEE 802.1d Spanning Tree
notes:
The first step of STP is to elect the root bridge, the reference of the whole topology. Bridges exchange BPDUs carrying the Bridge ID, made of a 2-byte priority field and the 6-byte base MAC, and the lowest value wins: the Enterasys default is 0x8000 (32768), so with equal priorities the lowest MAC wins. Then each segment gets a path cost, which 802.1D-1998 recommends in inverse proportion to link speed; the table in the original notes (250, 100, 62, 19, 4, 2 for 4, 10, 16, 100, 1000 and 10000 Mbps) gives the costs recommended in the original course, and on the equipment set spantree legacypathcost enable selects the 802.1D-1998 values, while the default uses the 802.1t-2001 ones. 2026 update: with 802.1t and 802.1w, now in 802.1Q-2022, the bridge priority is a multiple of 4096, from 0 to 61440, and the port cost goes from 1 to 200000000 instead of 1 to 65535; in the CLI this corresponds to the 802.1t mode of the priority (default on SecureStack, while the legacy 8021d mode accepts 0 to 65535) and to legacy path cost disabled. Tip: define the root bridge on purpose, lowering the priority of the core switch, instead of letting the MAC decide.
