slides.title: IEEE 802.1d Spanning Tree
notes:
This slide summarizes the six steps of 802.1d: elect the root bridge, assign path costs, determine the designated bridge of each segment (the one offering the lowest cost to the root, breaking ties by the lowest Bridge ID), identify the root and designated ports, block the redundant ports and maintain the topology with BPDUs. Root and designated ports stay in forwarding; the redundant ones stay in blocking but keep receiving BPDUs. The default timers are hello 2 s, max age 20 s and forward delay 15 s, dictated by the root, and the 802.1d states are disabled, blocking, listening, learning and forwarding. Since the forward delay is the time a port spends in each of the listening and learning states, it takes about 30 s (2 × 15 s) to reach forwarding, and up to about 50 s if it first has to wait for the 20 s max age (an estimate from the timers); meanwhile no port forwards data, and this window is the big problem of the original 802.1d. 2026 update: the 2-byte Port ID (1 byte of priority and 1 of port number) is the 802.1D-1998 one; with 802.1t and 802.1w the port priority is a multiple of 16, from 0 to 240, which is the range the CLI accepts.

[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), set spantree bridgeprioritymode 8021d: legacy bridge priority values 0 to 65535 (p. 6-34, PDF p. 486) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

notes:

In the last animation the letters R (root port) and D (designated port) mark the ports that stay in forwarding, and the redundant links are blocked. Tip: on the equipment, if the Designated Root MacAddr of show spantree stats equals the Bridge ID MAC Address, the bridge considers itself the root and has no root port.

slides.title: 802.1w, Rapid Spanning Tree
notes:
RSTP (802.1w) is an evolution of 802.1d that greatly reduces the time to reconfigure the topology and interoperates with STP. When the port comes up, the switch starts a three-second migration timer, sends RSTP BPDUs and then speaks the version matching the next BPDU received, that is, STP if the neighbor is 802.1d. On that connection 802.1d rules apply, so depending on where the failure occurs the recovery times will be those of RSTP or those of 802.1d. The explicit handshake of the rapid transition only happens on point-to-point (full duplex) links; on shared segments it is not used. 2026 update: 802.1w was incorporated into 802.1D-2004 and is now part of IEEE 802.1Q-2022. Tip: if convergence is slow, look for a neighbor still running 802.1d or an inter-switch link that is not in full duplex.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Spanning Tree Configuration Summary, RSTP: evolution of 802.1D with much faster convergence, explicit handshake between new root port and designated port (p. 6-1, PDF p. 235) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Spanning Tree point-to-point set to auto by default (Table 2-1, p. 2-5, PDF p. 31) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[3] IEEE 802.1 Working Group: 802.1D-2003 revision project page (published as 802.1D-2004; incorporates 802.1t and 802.1w; removes the Spanning Tree Protocol of Clause 8), Project scope: incorporate 802.1t and 802.1w into 802.1D. https://www.ieee802.org/1/pages/802.1D-2003.html
[4] IEEE Std 802.1Q-2022, IEEE Standard for Local and Metropolitan Area Networks--Bridges and Bridged Networks, IEEE 802.1Q-2022 standard page: Active Standard; RSTP among the keywords. https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/802.1Q/10323/
[5] Cisco: Understanding Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1w), Sections Compatibility with 802.1D, Link Type and Convergence with 802.1w. https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/lan-switching/spanning-tree-protocol/24062-146.html

slides.title: 802.1w, Rapid Spanning Tree
notes:
RSTP cuts the recovery from the 30 to 50 seconds of 802.1d (an estimate from the timers: 2 × 15 s of forward delay, plus the 20 s of max age when it has to be waited for) to about 3 times the hello, that is, 6 s with the default 2 s hello, when the bridge stops receiving BPDUs, and up to a few hundred milliseconds in well-configured networks. The election is still of a single root bridge, and the bridges compare the BPDUs they receive to compute the shortest path to it; what changes is that the roles (root, designated, alternate, backup) are assigned to each port individually, and it is not a tree per port. Topology Change Notifications also change: in 802.1d the bridge tells the root, which sets the TC flag in the BPDUs and makes the other bridges shorten the address table aging time to the forward delay, and in RSTP the bridge that detects the change spreads it out of its root and designated ports. On Enterasys equipment user ports rapidly transition to forwarding by default. Tip: the gain only appears with point-to-point links and no 802.1d bridges in the path.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Spanning Tree Configuration Summary, RSTP: port roles assigned to individual ports; user ports rapidly transition to forwarding by default (p. 6-1, PDF p. 235); defaults hello 2 s, forward delay 15 s, maximum aging time 20 s (Table 1-1, p. 1-4, PDF p. 38) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] RFC 4188: Definitions of Managed Objects for Bridges (Bridge MIB), dot1dStpForwardDelay (time in each of Listening and Learning; also used to age all dynamic Forwarding Database entries during a topology change); dot1dStpMaxAge. https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4188
[3] Cisco: Understanding Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1w), Sections Convergence with 802.1D (twice the forward delay), Conclusion (RSTP convergence sometimes a few hundred milliseconds), Topology Change Mechanisms (802.1D: TCN notifies the root, the TC flag is set, aging reduced to forward delay seconds; RSTP: the initiator floods the TC on all designated ports and the root port), Port Roles. https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/lan-switching/spanning-tree-protocol/24062-146.html

slides.title: 802.1w, Rapid Spanning Tree
notes:
RSTP assigns a role to each port: the root port is the only port of the bridge that leads to the root bridge (the one that receives the best BPDU, elected by the lowest path cost); the designated port offers the path to the root for the segment or the downstream bridge; the alternate is an alternative path to the root through another bridge and is blocked; the backup receives better BPDUs from its own bridge, that is, it is a redundant attachment to a segment that already has another port of the same bridge, and it is blocked; and the edge port has no other bridges, like user ports. The role is assigned by the protocol and determines the behavior of the port, that is, whether it sends or receives BPDUs and whether it forwards or blocks data (Matrix N guide), and the state of the port (Discarding, Learning or Forwarding) follows from it, which is the subject of the next slide. On the equipment, show spantree stats port shows the role and state of each port. Tip: configure user ports as edge and remember that an edge port that receives a BPDU loses that status.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Spanning Tree Configuration Summary, RSTP: assigns port roles to individual ports (p. 6-1, PDF p. 235); set spantree adminedge (pp. 6-38 and 6-39, PDF pp. 272-273) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Table 6-2, Port-Specific show spantree stats Output Details: the Role field is assigned by the protocol and determines whether the port sends or receives BPDUs and forwards or blocks data traffic (p. 6-13, PDF p. 465) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[3] Cisco: Understanding Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1w), Sections Port Roles (root, designated, alternate, backup) and Edge Ports (an edge port that receives a BPDU loses edge status). https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/lan-switching/spanning-tree-protocol/24062-146.html

slides.title: 802.1w, Rapid Spanning Tree
notes:
Ports with the root and designated roles are part of the active topology and therefore forward traffic; alternate and backup ports stay outside it, blocked, and serve as redundant connectivity in case a root or designated port fails. In the slide example, the switch in blue has two designated ports, one root, one alternate and one backup: if the root port fails, the alternate can become the new root port and transition to forwarding by explicit handshake, without waiting for the 802.1d timers. RSTP merges the disabled, blocking and listening states of 802.1d into a single Discarding state, which discards frames and does not learn MAC addresses, and keeps Learning, which already learns addresses, and Forwarding. On the equipment the State field of show spantree stats lists Blocking, Forwarding, Listening and Learning, and Discarding is not on that list in the Matrix N guide. Tip: remind students that the role dictates the state, not the other way round.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), Spanning Tree Configuration Summary, RSTP: a new root port and the designated port on the other side transition to forwarding through an explicit handshake (p. 6-1, PDF p. 235) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Table 6-2: State field can be Blocking, Forwarding, Listening or Learning (p. 6-13, PDF p. 465); Table 6-2 Role field: the role determines whether the port sends or receives BPDUs and forwards or blocks data traffic (p. 6-13, PDF p. 465) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[3] Cisco: Understanding Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1w), Sections Port States (the 802.1D disabled, blocking and listening states are merged into discarding; table of states: discarding does not learn MAC addresses, learning and forwarding do) and Port Roles (alternate and backup ports are blocked). https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/lan-switching/spanning-tree-protocol/24062-146.html

slides.title: 802.1w, Rapid Spanning Tree
notes:
This slide summarizes how RSTP handles topology changes (TC) and the clearing of the address table. In RSTP only a non-edge port that moves to forwarding generates a TC; a port that moves to blocking does not. The bridge that detects the TC starts the TC While timer, sends BPDUs with the TC bit on its designated and root ports and clears the addresses learned on them; the bridge that receives the TC clears the addresses learned on all ports, except the one that received it, and relays it, and RSTP also handles the 802.1d TCNs when legacy neighbors exist. After a TC the addresses have to be relearned, so the Topology Change Count of show spantree stats should not grow in a stable network. Tip: configure all user ports as edge, so that plugging and unplugging PCs does not generate TCs.

[3] Cisco: Understanding Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1w), Section New Topology Change Mechanisms (Topology Change Detection and Topology Change Propagation): only non-edge ports moving to forwarding cause a TC; a port that moves to blocking no longer generates a TC; TC While timer; MAC addresses flushed; propagation on all designated ports and root port. https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/lan-switching/spanning-tree-protocol/24062-146.html

slides.title: 802.1w, Rapid Spanning Tree
notes:
These are the basic Spanning Tree commands on both devices. The default version is mstp, compatible and interoperable with 802.1d and RSTP; stpcompatible makes the bridge transmit only 802.1d BPDUs and prevents non-edge ports from transitioning rapidly, which is why in most networks it is not changed. To turn the protocol on or off, SecureStack uses set spantree {disable | enable} and the Matrix N uses set spantree stpmode {none | ieee8021}, and per port set spantree portadmin works on both. The port priority goes from 0 to 240 in steps of 16 (0 is the highest), and the administrative port cost (adminpathcost) goes from 0 to 200000000, or from 0 to 65535 if legacy path cost is enabled, with 0 being the value that makes the port recalculate the cost from its speed. Backup root makes a bridge directly connected to the root dynamically lower its own priority and take over if the root is lost, preventing stale Spanning Tree information from circulating; the Matrix N guide says it is enabled on those bridges, while the SecureStack guide example shows backup root disabled, so check with show spantree backuproot. Tip: adjust the priority of the core bridge first and only then touch portpri and adminpathcost.

slides.title: 802.1w, Rapid Spanning Tree
notes:
Use show spantree stats to see the Spanning Tree state: the guide example with no arguments shows only the global parameters and, with the port keyword, also the port table (SID, Port, State, Role, Cost and Priority); the active option lists only the ports that have already received BPDUs. The Root Max Age, Root Hello Time and Root Forward Delay fields are the root values, and the Bridge ones are local; the defaults are 20, 2 and 15 seconds. In the slide example, ge.2.1 and ge.2.4 have cost 20000 and ge.2.2 and ge.2.3 have 200000: since the recommended cost is in inverse proportion to link speed, the larger cost indicates a slower link. Tip: Topology Change Count and Time Since Top Change show whether the topology is stable.

slides.title: 802.1w, Rapid Spanning Tree
notes:

slides.title: Span Guard™
notes:
Span Guard protects user ports against BPDUs: a user device does not need to run STP, and a malicious or misconfigured device sending BPDUs may try to take over the root role or destabilize the topology. 802.1d takes about 30 to 50 seconds to recover (an estimate from the timers) and RSTP much less, from a few seconds to hundreds of milliseconds, but repeated TCs and new root announcements can still cause denial of service, because each TC makes the switches clear their address table entries. With Span Guard, a port defined as edge that receives a non-loopback BPDU is locked in blocking and the manager is warned by trap. The concept is equivalent to the BPDU Guard of other vendors, which puts the port in errdisable; there is no IEEE or IETF standard for this feature, since 802.1Q only defines that an edge port stops being edge when it receives a BPDU. Tip: turn Span Guard on only after defining which ports are ISLs and which are user ports (next slide).

slides.title: Blocking BPDU attacks
notes:
With Span Guard enabled, a BPDU received on an edge port (except a loopback one) locks the port in blocking, which is why forged BPDUs cause neither topology changes nor new respans. The port returns when the global timeout expires (spanguardtimeout, default 300 s, from 0 to 65535, and 0 keeps the port locked until it is unlocked manually) or when the administrator unlocks it with clear spantree spanguardlock. The warning is an SNMP trap controlled by set spantree spanguardtrapenable, which is enabled by default on SecureStack. To check, use show spantree spanguard (enabled or disabled), show spantree spanguardlock (port locked or unlocked) and show spantree spanguardtimeout. The Matrix N guide describes the effect as disabling the port and the SecureStack one as the blocking state; the slide follows the SecureStack one. Tip: a hub or switch plugged by mistake into a user port locks the port, so check show spantree spanguardlock and, once the cause is removed, unlock the port instead of waiting for the timer.

slides.title: Deploying Span Guard ™
notes:
Span Guard is global, not per port: it is enabled with set spantree spanguard enable (the default is disabled) and it acts on the ports with adminedge TRUE. That is why the most important step is to separate the ports: set spantree adminedge port-string false on the links between switches (ISLs) before enabling, and true on the user ports you want to protect. The SecureStack guide explains that adminedge starts as false after power up and becomes true if no BPDU arrives on the port within a few seconds, so do not let an ISL depend on that automatic detection. The port stays locked for the global time of set spantree spanguardtimeout (default 300 s; 0 locks until manually unlocked), and set or clear spantree spanguardlock unlocks it at once, overriding the timeout. It is also unlocked if Span Guard is disabled or the port stops being an edge port. Tip: the Matrix N guide does not give the default value of adminedge, so check each port with show spantree adminedge before enabling.

slides.title: Lab: Spanning Tree and SpanGuard ™
notes:
Configure RSTP with set spantree version rstp (the default is mstp), build the redundant connections and, before confirming with show spantree stats port, predict on which port blocking will occur: the root is the bridge with the lowest Bridge ID and each bridge picks the lowest-cost path to it. The Role column of that output gives the role of each port (step c). In step d, disconnect and reconnect ports with different roles (root, alternate, designated) and use Wireshark to see the BPDUs with the topology change bit, comparing with the Topology Change Count. In step e, measure the reconvergence time by switching off the root bridge and watch which bridge becomes the new root (Designated Root MacAddr in show spantree stats). In steps f and g, set adminedge false on the ISLs, enable Span Guard and connect a switch running STP to a user port: the port should become locked in blocking, with a trap, and show spantree spanguardlock shows the state. Tip: before step g, confirm with show spantree adminedge that the port is edge, otherwise Span Guard does not act.

Rule from the original 2007 program: after each lab, save the configuration named after the lab and the bench number.

slides.title: IP Communications: Internet Protocol
notes:
Every IP device, host or router, performs two steps before transmitting: determine the route (the next hop) and resolve the link-layer address of that next hop (ARP for IPv4 over Ethernet). The sentence "every host is a router" was adjusted: a host makes routing decisions using its routing table, but it only forwards other nodes' packets if it is configured to act as a gateway. In operation this explains why a PC without a gateway can only talk to its own subnet. 2026 update: in IPv6 the ARP function is performed by Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861), but the two-step logic is the same. Tip: use the "route print" or "ip route" output of a PC as a concrete example.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Communication Layers (STD 3), Section 3.3.1.1 Local/Remote Decision (host chooses direct delivery or a gateway from its routing table) and Section 3.2.1.3 (a host silently discards datagrams not addressed to it unless it acts as a gateway). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122
[2] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Introduction and Packet Generation (resolve the protocol address of the next hop to a 48-bit Ethernet address). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826
[3] RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6), Section 7.2 Address Resolution (IPv6 equivalent of ARP). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4861

slides.title: IP Addressing
notes:
An IPv4 address is 32 bits long, written as four octets separated by dots (dotted-decimal notation). Every address has a network part and a host part, and the boundary is defined by the mask (prefix) associated with the address. That is why an address should never be interpreted without its mask. 2026 update: the same idea applies in IPv6, with 128 bits and a 64-bit prefix on LAN subnets (RFC 4291). Tip: ask a student which network 10.1.1.200/26 belongs to, without a calculator.

Sources:
[1] RFC 791: Internet Protocol (STD 5), Section 3.2 Discussion (addresses are 32 bits; network number and local address). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc791
[2] RFC 950: Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure (STD 5), Section 2.1 Interpretation of Internet Addresses (subnet mask defines the split). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc950
[3] RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan (BCP 122), Section 3.1 Basic Concept and Prefix Notation. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632
[4] RFC 4291: IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture, Section 2.5.4 Global Unicast Addresses (n-bit subnet prefix plus interface ID, 64 bits). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291

slides.title: Binary
notes:
Binary review: each bit is 1 (yes) or 0 (no) and each position of an octet weighs 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Eight set bits add up to 255, seven set bits on the left add up to 254, and the pattern 11110000 is 128+64+32+16 = 240. In operation, these are exactly the values (128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254, 255) that appear in subnet masks. Tip: have the class memorize that sequence, because it avoids a calculator during troubleshooting.

Sources:
[1] RFC 791: Internet Protocol (STD 5), Section 3.2 Discussion (addresses as bit fields of 8-bit octets). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc791

slides.title: Subnet mask
notes:
The subnet mask separates the network part from the host part and does not have to match an octet boundary. It can be written in decimal (255.255.255.0) or in prefix/CIDR notation (/24, the number of consecutive 1 bits). The network part is obtained by a bitwise AND between the address and the mask; the remaining bits form the host part. 2026 update: the /n notation and the contiguous-mask rule are those of RFC 4632; classes are no longer used to choose the mask. Tip: when you see a decimal mask, convert it to /n first.

Sources:
[1] RFC 950: Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure (STD 5), Section 2.2 Changes to Host Software to Support Subnets (bitwise_and of address and mask). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc950
[2] RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Communication Layers (STD 3), Section 3.3.1.1 Local/Remote Decision (compare destination and own address under the mask). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122
[3] RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan (BCP 122), Section 3.1 Basic Concept and Prefix Notation. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632
[4] RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, Section 2.2.5.2 Classless Inter Domain Routing (CIDR). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812

slides.title: IP address classes
notes:
The slides show classful addressing: class A (/8), B (/16) and C (/24), where the first octet decided the default mask. This was correct in 2007 as a teaching starting point, but it is historical. 2026 update: since CIDR (RFC 1519, now RFC 4632) addressing is classless and the mask is independent of the first octet; "class" survives only in expressions such as "class C network" and in class D (multicast). In operation, always check the configured prefix and never assume it from the class. Tip: show a /27 or a /22 to prove that classes are not enough.

Sources:
[1] RFC 791: Internet Protocol (STD 5), Section 3.2 Discussion, Addressing (classes A, B and C). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc791
[2] RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, Section 2.2.5.1 Classical IP Addressing Architecture and Section 2.2.5.2 Classless Inter Domain Routing (CIDR). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812
[3] RFC 1519: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), obsoleted by RFC 4632, Abstract and Section 1 (introduction of CIDR, 1993; obsoleted by RFC 4632). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1519
[4] RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan (BCP 122), Section 2 History and Problem Description; Section 3 Classless Addressing as a Solution. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632

slides.title: The binary AND operation   (boolean AND)
notes:
The Boolean AND operation: 1 AND X = X and 0 AND X = 0. The result is 1 only when both bits are 1. It is the tool that combines address and mask on the next slide. Tip: tell the class that the mask works like a "filter": where there is a 1 the address bit passes through; where there is a 0 the result is always 0.

Sources:
[1] RFC 950: Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure (STD 5), Section 2.2 Changes to Host Software to Support Subnets (bitwise_and in the local/remote test). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc950

slides.title: Determining the network with a “bitwise AND”
notes:
Full example: 172.16.128.195/24 in binary is 10000110.10001101.10000000.11000011; applying the mask 255.255.255.0 (24 one-bits) gives the network 172.16.128.0. Show bit by bit that the first three octets pass through and the last one is cleared. 2026 update: 172.16.0.0/16 is registered to Extreme Networks (inherited from the Enterasys material); in classes and documentation use the blocks reserved for documentation (RFC 5737) or the private ones (RFC 1918). Tip: redo the calculation with /26 so the class sees the network change to 172.16.128.192.

Sources:
[1] RFC 950: Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure (STD 5), Section 2.2 Changes to Host Software to Support Subnets (bitwise_and). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc950
[2] RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan (BCP 122), Section 3.1 Basic Concept and Prefix Notation. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632
[3] RFC 5737: IPv4 Address Blocks Reserved for Documentation, Section 3 Documentation Address Blocks (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5737
[4] RFC 1918: Address Allocation for Private Internets (BCP 5), Section 3 Private Address Space. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918
[5] ARIN RDAP: registration record for 134.141.0.0/16 (Extreme Networks), Registration record for NetRange 134.141.0.0 - 134.141.255.255. https://rdap.arin.net/registry/ip/134.141.0.0

slides.title: Route Determination
notes:
Determining the route means finding the next hop for a packet. If the destination is on a directly connected network (same subnet as the host, comparing the AND of each address with the mask), the next hop is the destination itself and the host ARPs for it directly. In operation, a wrong mask on a host makes it believe a remote destination is local and ARP for it, which explains many "I cannot ping" cases with no obvious cause. Tip: ask the class to test this conclusion with two PCs configured with different masks.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Communication Layers (STD 3), Section 3.3.1.1 Local/Remote Decision. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122
[2] RFC 950: Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure (STD 5), Section 2.2 Changes to Host Software to Support Subnets (bitwise_and test, direct delivery or gateway). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc950
[3] RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, Section 5.2.4.3 Next Hop Address. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812

slides.title: Route Determination
notes:
When the destination is not on the local network, the host consults the routing table and sends the packet to a router. The process has three steps: find the candidate routes, keep the most specific ones and, among those, choose the best. The sentence about the "closest router" was completed: the most specific route (longest mask) wins first and the metric only breaks ties between equivalent routes. The default route (0.0.0.0/0) is the last resort. Tip: use the table on slide 14 to show which destination would match the default and which would match a more specific route.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, Section 5.2.4.3 Next Hop Address: pruning rules (1) Basic Match, (2) Longest Match, (3) Weak TOS, (4) Best Metric, (5) Vendor Policy; and the Default Route discussion. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812
[2] RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Communication Layers (STD 3), Section 3.3.1.1 Local/Remote Decision and Section 3.3.1.2 Gateway Selection. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122

slides.title: The Route Selection Process
notes:
The flowchart summarizes the route pruning of RFC 1812: 1) a route is a candidate if the AND of the destination with its mask equals its network; 2) among the candidates, the one with the longest mask (most specific) wins; 3) among those left, the one with the lowest metric wins. If more than one remains, the final choice depends on the implementation (for example, ECMP load sharing). The metric is only comparable between routes of the same protocol; between different protocols the administrative distance (preference) decides, covered on slides 66 and 67. Tip: run the exercise with the table on slide 14 and any destination.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, Section 5.2.4.3 Next Hop Address (Basic Match, Longest Match, Best Metric, Vendor Policy) and Section 5.2.4.4 Administrative Preference. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812
[2] RFC 950: Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure (STD 5), Section 2.2 Changes to Host Software to Support Subnets (bitwise_and). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc950

slides.title: The Routing Table
notes:
The routing table of a PC shows network, mask, gateway, interface and metric. Reading example: for destination 172.16.75.20, the route 172.16.0.0/16 (connected) and the default 0.0.0.0/0 both match; the /16 wins because it is more specific. The /32 lines are the host itself and the directed broadcast, and 224.0.0.0 with mask 240.0.0.0 (/4) is the multicast range, corrected on the slide (the mask was shown as 224.0.0.0). In operation, the table comes from manual configuration, automatic configuration (DHCP) and routing protocols. Tip: ask a student for "route print" or "ip route" output and compare it with the slide.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, Section 5.2.4.3 Next Hop Address (Longest Match). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812
[2] RFC 1112: Host Extensions for IP Multicasting (STD 5), Section 4 Host Group Addresses (class D: high-order four bits 1110, 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255, i.e. 224.0.0.0/4). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1112
[3] ARIN RDAP: registration record for 134.141.0.0/16 (Extreme Networks), Registration record for 134.141.0.0/16 (public block of Extreme Networks, used here as an example). https://rdap.arin.net/registry/ip/134.141.0.0

slides.title: ARP: Address Resolution Protocol
notes:
ARP (RFC 826, STD 37) resolves a protocol address (IPv4) into a link-layer address (Ethernet MAC) on the same local network. It has its own packet format, does not use the IP header and is identified by EtherType 0x0806; that is why it is not part of IP and does not perform route determination. 2026 update: in IPv6 ARP was replaced by Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861); RFC 826 was updated by RFC 5227 (address conflict detection) and RFC 5494 (IANA registries). Tip: in a packet analyzer filter on "arp" to show live requests.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Title, Introduction and Packet format (RFC 826 is Internet Standard STD 37, updated by RFC 5227 and RFC 5494). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826
[2] RFC 894: A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over Ethernet Networks (STD 41), Frame format: type field 0x0806 identifies ARP. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc894
[3] RFC 4861: Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6), Section 7.2 Address Resolution (IPv6 replacement for ARP). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4861
[4] IANA: IEEE 802 Numbers (EtherType registry), EtherType 0x0806 = Address Resolution Protocol (ARP); 0x0800 = IPv4. https://www.iana.org/assignments/ieee-802-numbers/ieee-802-numbers.xhtml

slides.title: Anatomy of an ARP packet
notes:
The ARP packet is carried directly inside an Ethernet II (DIX) frame: destination MAC, source MAC, EtherType 0x0806, data and FCS. The ARP fields are: hardware type (16 bits), protocol type (16), hardware address length (8), protocol address length (8), operation code (16) and four variable-length addresses (source and target, hardware and protocol). For Ethernet/IPv4 this adds up to 28 octets, which the frame pads up to the 46-octet minimum data field required by RFC 894. Tip: counting the 28 octets in a real capture helps fix the format.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet format (ar$hrd 16 bits, ar$pro 16, ar$hln 8, ar$pln 8, ar$op 16, then ar$sha, ar$spa, ar$tha, ar$tpa). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826
[2] RFC 894: A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over Ethernet Networks (STD 41), Frame format: minimum data field of 46 octets, padded if necessary; type 0x0806 for ARP. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc894
[3] IANA: IEEE 802 Numbers (EtherType registry), EtherType 0x0806 = ARP. https://www.iana.org/assignments/ieee-802-numbers/ieee-802-numbers.xhtml

slides.title: Field: Hardware Type
notes:
Hardware Type field (16 bits): indicates the physical and data-link technology. Ethernet is 0x0001. The IANA registry lists other values for other technologies.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet format: ar$hrd, ares_hrd$Ethernet = 1. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826
[2] IANA: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) Parameters, Hardware Type registry: 1 = Ethernet (10Mb). https://www.iana.org/assignments/arp-parameters/arp-parameters.xhtml

slides.title: Field: Protocol Type
notes:
Protocol Type field (16 bits): identifies the network protocol whose addresses are being resolved. It uses the same values as the EtherType; IP (IPv4) is 0x0800.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet format: ar$pro (same values as the Ethernet type field). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826
[2] IANA: IEEE 802 Numbers (EtherType registry), EtherType 0x0800 = IPv4. https://www.iana.org/assignments/ieee-802-numbers/ieee-802-numbers.xhtml

slides.title: Field: Hardware address length
notes:
Hardware Address Length field (8 bits): gives, in octets, the size of the link-layer address. For Ethernet it is 6 octets (48 bits).

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet format: ar$hln, "length in bytes of each hardware address" (6 for Ethernet). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: Field: Protocol address length
notes:
Protocol Address Length field (8 bits): gives, in octets, the size of the network-layer address. For IPv4 it is 4 octets.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet format: ar$pln, "length in bytes of each protocol address" (4 for IPv4). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: Field: Operational Code (OP_Code)
notes:
Operation Code field, OP_Code (16 bits): 1 is a request (REQUEST) and 2 is a reply (REPLY, called "Response" on the slide). It is the field the receiver checks to decide whether it should answer. The IANA registry also lists other codes (for example RARP and InARP), outside the scope of the course.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet format: ar$op, ares_op$REQUEST = 1, ares_op$REPLY = 2. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826
[2] IANA: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) Parameters, Operation Code registry: 1 REQUEST, 2 REPLY. https://www.iana.org/assignments/arp-parameters/arp-parameters.xhtml

slides.title: Fields: Hardware Address
notes:
Source and target hardware address fields (6 octets each on Ethernet). In a request the target hardware address is precisely what is being discovered; RFC 826 says it needs no particular value and in practice stacks and RFC 5227 use zeros, which is why the slide was changed from "is made up of zeros" to "is usually made up of zeros". The Ethernet frame carrying the request, by contrast, is sent to broadcast (ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff). Tip: in the analyzer, show the "target MAC" 00:00:00:00:00:00 in a request.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation: the requester "does not set ar$tha to anything in particular"; Packet Reception (ar$tha = "don't care" in the request). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826
[2] RFC 5227: IPv4 Address Conflict Detection, Section 2.1.1 ARP Probe (target hardware address "ignored and SHOULD be set to all zeroes"). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5227

slides.title: Fields: Protocol Address
notes:
Source and target protocol address fields (4 octets each for IPv4). ARP answers the question: I know the protocol address (for example IP), what is the physical address I should send the frame to? In a request, the source protocol address is the asker's and the target protocol address is the IP being resolved.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet format (ar$spa, ar$tpa) and Packet Generation. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: ARP: Address Resolution Protocol
notes:
Scenario of the ARP sequence: stations A, B and C are on the same network 172.16.128.0/16 and A wants to talk to C. The letters A, B and C stand for the MAC addresses, for illustration only. Ask the class what A already knows (C's IP) and what is still missing (C's MAC).

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception (the algorithm illustrated on this slide). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: ARP: Address Resolution Protocol
notes:
A sends an ARP request as a link-layer broadcast (destination MAC ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff) asking who has C's IP. B and C both receive the frame, because a broadcast reaches every station on the local network. The request already carries A's IP and MAC as the source.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception (the algorithm illustrated on this slide). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: ARP: Address Resolution Protocol
notes:
C recognizes that the IP being sought is its own and stores the association A's IP to A's MAC in its ARP cache. B notices that the request is not for it and discards the packet (RFC 826 only has B update A's entry if one already exists in B's cache). This learning of the sender avoids a second request from C to A.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception (the algorithm illustrated on this slide). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: ARP: Address Resolution Protocol
notes:
C checks the OP_Code: since it is a request, it answers with an ARP reply sent as unicast straight to A's MAC, giving its own MAC. The reply is not broadcast.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception (the algorithm illustrated on this slide). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: ARP: Address Resolution Protocol
notes:
A receives the reply, recognizes that it is addressed to it, and stores the association C's IP to C's MAC in its ARP cache. From here A can build the Ethernet frame for C.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception (the algorithm illustrated on this slide). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: ARP: Address Resolution Protocol
notes:
A checks the OP_Code: since the packet received is a reply, A does not send another reply to C. This operation-code test is what prevents an endless loop of requests and replies.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception (the algorithm illustrated on this slide). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: ARP: Address Resolution Protocol
notes:
A and C now have each other's protocol address (IP) and hardware address (MAC) and can exchange data. In operation these entries expire: RFC 1122 requires a mechanism to age out ARP cache entries, and on the Enterasys switch-routers the default time is 14,400 seconds (slide 71). 2026 update: IP address conflicts are detected using ARP Probe and Announcement (RFC 5227). Tip: if a machine changes its network card and loses communication for minutes or hours, suspect a stale ARP cache entry on the router.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C2 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.00.xx, P/N 9033991-14 (June 2007), Chapter 1 default settings (ARP timeout 14,400 seconds), p. 1-5 (PDF p. 35) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Section 2.1 default settings (ARP timeout 14,400 seconds), p. 2-7 (PDF p. 33) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[3] RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts - Communication Layers (STD 3), Section 2.3.2.1 ARP Cache Validation (MUST provide a way to flush out-of-date entries). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122
[4] RFC 5227: IPv4 Address Conflict Detection, Section 2.1 Probing an Address / Section 2.3 Announcing an Address. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5227

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
Proxy ARP lets hosts that do not understand subnets keep working: the router answers the ARP on behalf of the destination, which is on another subnet, using its own MAC. The origin, given as "1985", was adjusted: RFC 925 (1984) already describes the idea, RFC 950 (1985) standardizes subnetting, and RFC 1027 (1987) documents Proxy ARP in subnet gateways. On the devices the feature is per interface (command ip proxy-arp): the Matrix N DFE guide says it is enabled by default, the SecureStack C2 guide says it is disabled by default. Tip: on current networks prefer correct masks on the hosts and disable Proxy ARP when it is not needed.

Sources:
[1] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx (Matrix N-Series DFE), P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), Section 12.2.4.5 ip proxy-arp, p. 12-25 (PDF p. 985): "It is enabled by default." (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] SecureStack C2 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.00.xx, P/N 9033991-14 (June 2007), ip proxy-arp, p. 15-11 (PDF p. 473): "Defaults: Disabled." (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[3] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Status of this Memo and Section 1 Motivation (based on RFC 950, RFC 922, RFC 826; a restricted subset of RFC 925). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027
[4] RFC 925: Multi-LAN Address Resolution (October 1984), Abstract and Introduction (multi-LAN address resolution, October 1984). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc925
[5] RFC 950: Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure (STD 5), Introduction (Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure, August 1985). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc950

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
Proxy ARP scenario: A (172.16.128.20/16) and B (172.16.64.30/16) use a /16 mask and therefore think they are on the same network, but Router 1 separates them into two /24 subnets (172.16.128.1/24 and 172.16.64.1/24). From its routing table, A believes B is a directly reachable next hop. Tip: ask the class to spot the mask mismatch in the drawing (hosts at /16, router at /24).

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method (gateway answers the ARP request on behalf of the target with its own hardware address); Section 2.2 Routing; Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
A sends an ARP request as a broadcast for B's IP. Because it is a broadcast, Router 1 receives it too and runs a decision process, shown on the next slide, to know whether it answers on behalf of B.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method (gateway answers the ARP request on behalf of the target with its own hardware address); Section 2.2 Routing; Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
The flowchart decides whether the router processes the ARP: it processes it if the target is the router itself; otherwise it only processes it if it has a route to the target network and that best route leaves through an interface different from the one on which the ARP arrived. Otherwise it discards the ARP. The different-interface rule prevents the router from answering for hosts that are on the same segment as the requester; RFC 1027 also says the default route must not be used for this decision, and that the gateway should not reply when the source and target IP networks differ. In operation, Proxy ARP only works if there is a specific route to the target.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C2 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.00.xx, P/N 9033991-14 (June 2007), ip proxy-arp, p. 15-11 (PDF p. 473) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.2 Routing (the default route must not be used for the check) and Section 2.4 Sanity checks (no reply if source and target are on the same physical network or on different IP networks). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
If it decides to process the ARP, Router 1 first stores the association A's IP to A's MAC in its ARP table, like any receiver of an ARP request.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027
[2] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
The router sees that the OP_Code is a request and answers A, but with B's IP associated with the router's own MAC. That is why it is said to answer "by proxy" for B.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027
[2] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
A receives the ARP reply and stores in its ARP table that B's IP corresponds to Router 1's MAC. For A everything looks normal: it thinks it has learned B's MAC.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
A starts transmitting packets with B's destination IP, but inside frames carrying Router 1's MAC. A believes it is communicating directly with B. Tip: in the analyzer, show a frame whose destination MAC is the router's and whose destination IP is B's.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
Through the route determination process, Router 1 sees that B is on its other IP interface and sends an ARP request for B out of interface 172.16.64.1. This ARP is only sent when a packet for B arrives at the router and it does not yet have a valid ARP entry for B (original course note).

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
B receives the router's request and stores in its ARP table the router's IP (172.16.64.1) associated with the router's MAC. B learns the router, not A.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
Since this was an ARP request sent by the router, B answers with a unicast ARP reply back to the router, giving its MAC.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
The router receives B's reply and stores B's MAC in its ARP table. It can now deliver A's packet to B.

Sources:
[1] RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol (STD 37), Packet Generation and Packet Reception. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc826

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
The router forwards to B the packet that A sent. As in any IP forwarding, the router decrements the TTL by at least one, so a traceroute from A to B would show the router as a hop.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, Section 5.3.1 Time to Live (TTL): a forwarding router MUST decrement the TTL by at least one. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
When B wants to reply to A, it also believes A is on the same network (/16 mask), so it ARPs for A's MAC as a broadcast. The router receives this broadcast, as it did on the way in.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
The router applies the same decision process to decide whether to answer by proxy for A: the target is on a different interface and there is a specific route to it.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
Having decided to answer, the router sends B an ARP reply carrying A's IP and the router's MAC. It is the same exchange as before, now in the opposite direction.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
B receives the ARP reply and stores in its table that A's IP corresponds to the router's MAC. B will therefore also send to the router everything destined for A.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

slides.title: Proxy-ARP
notes:
A and B can now communicate, each convinced that the other is on the same network, while the router does the connecting work behind the scenes. In operation, the typical symptom of Proxy ARP is the same MAC (the router's) appearing for several IPs in the hosts' ARP tables. Tip: use this pattern to recognize Proxy ARP when troubleshooting.

Sources:
[1] RFC 1027: Using ARP to Implement Transparent Subnet Gateways (October 1987), Section 2.1 Basic method and Section 2.4 Sanity checks. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1027

notes:

In the 2007 guides, routing on the Matrix N is enabled per module (set router) and on the SecureStack with the router command in su mode. The 2005 Matrix X guide confirms the device as a layer 2 switch (chapter 3) and a layer 3 router (chapter 4), with routing interfaces on physical ports, VLANs and loopbacks. The Matrix E1, shown on the next slide, also routes but is not on this list. Tip: ask the class which L3 devices they operate today and how each one enables routing.

slides.title: IP interfaces
notes:
Each routed VLAN gets an IP interface with a primary address and, optionally, secondary addresses (on the DFE, up to 50 secondary addresses per interface and 256 interfaces per module; on the Matrix X, up to 64 secondary addresses and 1024 interfaces). A newly created interface is administratively DOWN until the no shutdown command, and the Matrix X also allows addressing physical ports and loopbacks, which confirms the third item on the slide. The item about two interfaces on the same subnet appears in no guide, and the Matrix X guide describes interfaces with addresses on the same subnet, so it was replaced by the documented interface limits. Changes enter the running configuration immediately; on the SecureStack C2 the write to NVRAM is automatic (2 minutes on a standalone unit, 30 minutes on a stack) or immediate with save config. In the English version, "Atenção" was translated as "Attention". Tip: after creating the interface, check it with show ip interface.

slides.title: Host IP Interface
notes:
The host interface is the device's own IP address for management (Telnet, ping, SNMP) and is tied to a VLAN: on the SecureStack, set host vlan, show host vlan and clear host vlan (which returns to VLAN 1); on the Matrix N, the logical port host.0.1 is added to the VLAN with set port vlan and set vlan egress. The C2 and DFE guides describe this access as in-band, so the slide now says so and reserves the term out-of-band for the eth0 port of the Matrix X, a dedicated Ethernet management port on each control module. The C2 and DFE have separate commands for the host table in switch mode and for the router tables, which supports table independence on those platforms; on the Matrix X, however, the eth0 network appears in the routing table, and the statement was limited to the Matrix N and the SecureStack. The part "and is not reachable through it" appears in no guide and was removed. On the SecureStack, the host port address cannot fall within a routed interface that is already configured (C2 and C3 guides, DHCP server chapter). Tip: test access to the host IP from a routed VLAN and record the result.

slides.title: “Router” mode
notes:
To use the routing functions you must enter the router mode of the CLI. On the SecureStack you just type router in admin mode; on the Matrix N you first create the routing instance on the module (set router slot, done once) and then enter it (router slot). The 2007 guides and the vendor FAQ confirm up to two router instances in a DFE chassis (firmware up to 5.42.10), and the DFE guide says each routing module creates and maintains its own route tables. The expression "routing peers" and L3 redundancy between the instances appear in no guide and were removed from the slide. 2026 update: on firmware 6.01.01.0020 or higher the FAQ indicates only one instance. Tip: if the prompt does not change to router, check that the module was configured with set router.

slides.title: Basic configuration of router mode
notes:
The table shows the CLI modes of the SecureStack C2: switch mode (layer 2), router mode with the router> prompt, privileged router# mode, global configuration (configure), interface configuration (interface vlan) and protocol configuration (router rip or router ospf). The prompt column, which was shifted one row relative to the mode names, was corrected, and so were the commands cited: the command to clear ARP is clear arp-cache, and ping/traceroute are commands of the privileged router# mode. The sentence about limited functionality and some show commands at router> matches the guide, which allows show ip route and show ip arp in any router mode. The statement that switch mode shows the host routing table is not in the C2 guide, which documents show ip route only in router mode, and it was replaced by show arp, which shows the switch ARP table. IP interfaces used for routing must be tied to a VLAN already created on the switch. Tip: use exit to go up one level and remember that the prompt always shows the current mode.

slides.title: Step-by-step creation of an IP interface
notes:
Recipe to create a routed IP interface: create the VLAN, put the ports into it (PVID), add them to the egress list as untagged and remove them from the default VLAN; only then enter router mode and create the interface with address, mask and no shutdown. On the SecureStack C2 the global configuration command is configure and the interface prompt is router(Config-if(Vlan 1))#, a format we corrected on the slide. In operation, forgetting no shutdown is the most common cause of "the interface does not come up". Tip: confirm with show ip interface and with a ping from a host in the VLAN.

slides.title: Loopback interface configuration
notes:
The loopback interface is an internal IP interface that belongs to no VLAN and does not depend on the state of a physical port. It is created with interface loopback n in router mode, given an address and mask, and enabled with no shutdown, a step that appears in the preparation tables of the DFE and C2 guides. The guides confirm the three statements that previously had no source: the Matrix X guide says the loopback is useful for in-band management and as the default OSPF router ID, and that it is always up, and the DFE and C2 guides describe the loopback as always reachable. Its use as a stable router identifier (OSPF router-id, which only changes with a process restart, or BGP) requires it to be reachable by a static route or a routing protocol. The prompt was corrected to the guide format (Matrix>Router1). Tip: use a /32 mask and advertise the loopback address in OSPF.

slides.title: Static and dynamic routing support
notes:
Routing tables can be maintained statically (configured by hand) or dynamically (learned from other routers). By default, the static route wins over the dynamic one on the Matrix N and the SecureStack C2, because the default administrative distance is 1 against 110 (OSPF) and 120 (RIP) in the 2007 guides; on the Matrix X the default static distance is 60, and it loses to internal OSPF (10) and internal IS-IS (11). The two most widely used dynamic families are distance vector (RIP) and link state (OSPF), and the sentence was corrected to say that OSPF exchanges link-state advertisements, not route tables. In the capacity table, the Matrix N limit of 25,000 dynamic routes (the maximum of set router limits route-table, with 256 MB of memory) and the 2,048 static routes of the Matrix X are confirmed. The other values appear in no guide and were replaced by n/d, including the Matrix X "~265k", which matches neither the data sheet (RIB 512,000 and FIB 128,000) nor the release notes (100,000). Tip: before sizing a network, check the route limit of the firmware in use.

slides.title: Managing the routing table (the routes)
notes:
Every lookup in the routing table uses the destination address and returns the next hop and the outgoing interface. Routes can be static or dynamic, and dynamic protocols divide into distance vector (RIP v1 and v2, DVMRP for multicast), link state (OSPFv2, IS-IS) and path vector (BGP-4). We removed PIM-SM and PIM-SSM from the distance-vector list: PIM is "protocol independent", because it uses the existing unicast routing table to build multicast trees and does not exchange routes. 2026 update: RIPv1 (RFC 1058) is Historic and DVMRP is Experimental (RFC 1075). Tip: when classifying a protocol, ask what it advertises (distances, link states or AS paths).

slides.title: Route support on the devices
notes:
On the Matrix N DFE-Platinum each routing module supports up to 256 routing interfaces, each with RIP and/or OSPF, and when two routing modules are in the chassis each creates and maintains its own tables. OSPF and other advanced features require the advanced routing license: N-EOS-L3 on the Matrix N (one per chassis) and C2L3-LIC on the SecureStack C2 (applied once, for the standalone unit or the whole stack). Note: the C3 uses the C3L3-LIC license, which is node-locked to each unit, so the "one per stack" rule does not apply. Activation is done with license advanced in router mode (C2) or set license advanced in switch mode (Matrix N firmware 5.x), and the slide now shows both forms. Tip: verify with show license.

slides.title: Internal route management
notes:
The Route Table Manager (RTM) maintains the RIB (Route Information Base), which holds all active static routes, all RIP routes and up to three best OSPF routes per network. The RTM chooses up to three best routes per destination and installs them in the FIB (Forwarding Information Base), which is distributed to all modules so that the distributed forwarding engine decides right at the ingress port, when the frame arrives. We corrected the sentence about show ip route: the guide says it displays the IP route information (the routing table), not that it specifically shows the FIB. In operation, the three-route limit is what supports the load sharing on slide 70. Tip: use show ip route summary to see the total per protocol.

slides.title: Configuring static routes
notes:
The static route is configured with ip route prefix mask next-hop [distance]. On the Matrix X the syntax in the first line of the slide matches the 2005 command reference exactly, with the options tag, metric, unicast, multicast, noinstall, reject, retain and blackhole. The administrative distance goes from 1 to 255 and routes with a lower value are preferred; the default is 1 on the Matrix N and the SecureStack C2 but 60 on the Matrix X, so there the static route loses to internal OSPF (10) and internal IS-IS (11), and the slide was corrected at both points. The parameters in the list (vlan vlan-id, permanent and tag) come from the Matrix N DFE guide; the SecureStack C2 accepts only prefix, mask, next-hop address and distance, and the heading now says so. Tip: create a static default route (0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0) pointing to the domain gateway and check it with show ip route.

slides.title: Configuring the RIP routing protocol
notes:
RIP is a distance-vector protocol with hop count as its metric; RFC 1058 (RIPv1) is now Historic and RFC 2453 (RIPv2, STD 56) adds subnet masks (VLSM) and authentication, which the slide already mentions. To enable it the command is router rip on both devices, but the way to name the interfaces differs: on the Matrix N DFE you use network ip-address in router mode; on the SecureStack C2/C3 you use ip rip enable on the interface. We corrected the slide to show this difference. Tip: on the C2 the default is to send RIPv1 and accept v1 and v2; adjust it with ip rip send version and ip rip receive version.

slides.title: Enabling the OSPF routing protocol
notes:
OSPF is a link-state protocol based on Dijkstra's SPF algorithm, with fast reconvergence and load sharing across equal-cost paths (ECMP). In the 2007 guides only one OSPF process is allowed per routing module on the DFE and one per stack on the SecureStack, and the command is router ospf process-id; the slide did not show the mandatory argument and was corrected. OSPF requires a license (slide 61) and, after router ospf, you must specify networks and areas (network ... area ... or ip ospf enable on the interface). 2026 update: OSPFv2 is RFC 2328 (STD 54); for IPv6 the C3 already included ipv6 router ospf (OSPFv3). Tip: set the router-id from a loopback.

Put uplink and loopback in area 0: [2]
Passive interface (VLAN 10): [2]
Show neighbors: [3]

slides.title: Internal route precedence
notes:
This slide covers administrative distance (administrative distance in the Enterasys guides, administrative preference in RFC 1812): when more than one protocol offers the same destination network, the RTM installs the route with the lowest value. The default values in the 2007 guides are 0 for connected, 1 for static, 110 for OSPF and 120 for RIP. RFC 1812 (section 5.2.4.4) presents administrative preference as a suggested mechanism for the vendor policy rule, with values from 0 to 255 where 0 is the most preferred and 255 means never use, which is why the numbers differ between vendors. The phrase "for each entry in the table" was adjusted: in the guides the value is configured per protocol, per OSPF route type (intra-area, inter-area and external) and per static route in the ip route command. Tip: remind the class that distance only breaks ties between routes to the same prefix, because the more specific route already wins first (slide 12).

notes:

slides.title: Routing Table
notes:
The host interface is the switch's management address, and this table shows the default route via 192.168.0.1 (flags UGC), the host route for loopback 127.0.0.1 (UH) and the connected network 192.168.0.0 (UC); the Mask column is printed in hexadecimal (ffffff00 is 255.255.255.0). In the Matrix N DFE guide the flags are U (up), G (gateway), H (host route) and C (generate new routes on use), as listed in Table 11-12. The command is entered in switch mode, not router mode; the DFE guide documents this switch-level show ip route (section 11.2.5.6, with the Matrix(rw)-> prompt), but the SecureStack C2 guide documents show ip route only for router mode, so the prompt of the example was changed. The independence of the host interface table holds for the Matrix N and the SecureStack; on the Matrix X the eth0 network appears in the routing table. According to the original course note, interface host.0.1 has its own routing table and ARP cache, routing protocols on the VLAN interface do not change that table, ARP responses are split into two tables according to the interface that made the request, and the default route is only used with the host's own source address. Tip: ask the class why a managed switch needs a default route even when it does not route. The output shown is the DFE guide example, with the gateway replaced by the slide’s private address.

slides.title: ECMP: Multiple equal-cost paths
notes:
ECMP lets the router install more than one equal-cost path to the same destination and share traffic across them; RFC 2991 explains that per-packet round-robin can reorder packets and hurt TCP, and RFC 2992 describes hash-threshold, which keeps each flow on the same path. In the Matrix N DFE guide, the ip ecm-forwarding-algorithm command chooses between hash-thold (the default) and round-robin, and the RTM installs up to three best routes per network, determined by OSPF, in the FIB; the SecureStack C2 guide says the same, so the slide's figures of 8 and 4 were corrected to 3, while the 2006 DFE user's guide mentions four equal-cost OSPF or static routes. In the DFE and Matrix X guides round-robin installs flows alternately, not packets, and the slide text was adjusted. On the Matrix X, the 2005 guide describes multipath for OSPF and static routes (up to four routes) and the RIP ecmp command, disabled by default, and the data sheet mentions 8 paths; so the table shows "4 or 8": the guide documents up to four and the data sheet 8. The RIP mark of the Matrix N was changed to not supported, because the guides tie multipath to OSPF and static routes, and the cells that no guide confirms (C2 algorithms and static routes, Matrix X hashing) became n/d. Tip: show that with hashing, the same source/destination pair always uses the same path.

notes:

slides.title: Managing ARP
notes:
These are the ARP management commands: show arp (switch mode) shows the host ARP table, show ip arp (router mode) shows that of the VLAN interfaces, arp ip-address mac-address creates a static entry (up to 1,000 on the C2) and arp timeout seconds changes the lifetime of dynamic entries, from 0 to 65535 seconds, where 0 means never expire. The clear arp-cache command, entered at router#, deletes all dynamic entries and does not accept the [ip-address] parameter the slide showed, so the syntax was corrected (in the C2, C3 and DFE guides the command has no parameters; only the Matrix X has an optional IP, in its clear arp command). The 4 hours is the default (14,400 seconds) on both the C2 and the Matrix N, and the 6 hours of the Matrix X (21,600 seconds) is also a default and was confirmed in the 2005 command reference, so the label was adjusted to "default". RFC 1122 (section 2.3.2.1) requires a way to flush out-of-date ARP entries, which is why clearing the cache usually fixes problems after an address or network card change. Tip: show the old entry in show ip arp, clear the cache and show the new entry.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C2 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.00.xx, P/N 9033991-14 (June 2007), show arp (switch command), p. 11-17 (PDF p. 379); show ip arp, p. 15-8 and 15-9 (PDF pp. 470-471); arp ip-address mac-address (up to 1,000 static entries), p. 15-10 (PDF p. 472); arp timeout seconds, valid values 0 to 65535, default 14,400 seconds, p. 15-11 (PDF p. 473); clear arp-cache (no parameters, Privileged EXEC), p. 15-12 (PDF p. 474) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), clear arp-cache (Parameters: None; Privileged EXEC C3(su)->router#), p. 15-16 (PDF p. 470) (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

notes:
The router-mode show ip arp output lists the ARP entries of the VLAN interfaces, all on Vlan1, and the final line "Arp entry count = 13." matches the 13 rows of the table. The Dynamic entries show an age in minutes, from 0m to 141m, and the Internet entries with age "-" do not age: they are the router's own addresses 10.1.204.17, .65 and .97, with the same MAC 0001:F45F:49C5 seen on slide 72. The column layout and MAC notation differ from the C2 guide's example, which uses Internet in the Protocol column, a Type column and MACs such as 0003.4712.7a99, but the content of the slide is consistent. Since the default ageing time is 14,400 seconds (240 minutes), the 141-minute entry has not yet expired. Tip: ask the class to find the router's own three entries and explain why they do not age.

slides.title: ARP table
notes:
Side-by-side view of block B18. The full commands and the source of every line are on the vendor slides that follow.

• ARP is RFC 826 (STD 37, November 1982), identified by EtherType 0x0806. IPv6 has no ARP: Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) takes over that role.
• RFC 1122: ARP cache entries should expire (the listed approaches use about a minute) and large networks may need a longer timeout. Each device's default is vendor-specific.
• IPv4 address conflict detection uses the "ARP Probe": a broadcast ARP request with an all-zero sender IP address (RFC 5227).

slides.title: OSPF: link state and areas
notes:
This slide brings together the three ideas behind OSPF: every router knows the map of the area (the link-state database), calculates the shortest path to each destination by itself and uses areas to limit the size of that map. Routers in the same area have identical databases, and whatever joins two areas is the ABR, which keeps one database for each. Area 0 is the backbone and every other area attaches to it. In our lab topologies everything stays in area 0, which is the typical design of a small core. Tip: show in the routing table that OSPF does not carry the topology out of the area, only the prefixes summarized by the ABRs.

Sources:
[1] RFC 2328, OSPF Version 2 (STD 54), 1. Introduction; 1.1 Protocol overview; 3. Splitting the AS into Areas; 3.1 The backbone; A.1 Encapsulation of OSPF packets. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2328.txt

slides.title: OSPF: neighbor states, DR and BDR
notes:
The seven states tell the story of an adjacency: the Hello discovers the neighbor (Init), confirmation in both directions leads to 2-Way, and only then does the pair decide whether to become adjacent. In ExStart the routers choose the master, in Exchange they describe the database, in Loading they request what is missing and in Full they are synchronized. On broadcast networks, such as an Ethernet VLAN, the DR and BDR concentrate the adjacencies: the other routers stay in 2-Way with each other and Full only with the two. A router that arrives later accepts the existing DR even with a higher priority, so the election depends on the order in which the routers come up. Tip: on a broadcast VLAN, neighbors in 2-Way with each other are normal; if the pair with the DR or BDR does not reach Full, compare the MTU and the Hello parameters.

Sources:
[1] RFC 2328, OSPF Version 2 (STD 54), 7.1 The Hello Protocol; 7.3 The Designated Router; 7.4 The Backup Designated Router; 10.1 Neighbor states; 10.2 Events causing neighbor state changes; 10.3 The Neighbor state machine; 10.4 Whether to become adjacent; 10.5 Receiving Hello Packets; 10.6 Receiving Database Description Packets; Appendix C.3 Router Priority. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2328.txt

slides.title: OSPF: network types, cost and LSAs
notes:
Use this table as a reference card. The network type decides whether there is a DR election: it exists on broadcast and NBMA and not on point-to-point or point-to-multipoint, where routers always form an adjacency. That is why, on a routed link between two switches, setting the point-to-point type avoids the election and speeds up the neighbor coming up. The cost is a unitless metric: the RFC treats the cost as a parameter configured on each interface (appendix C.3) and each vendor defines its own default (on the C3 it is 10 on every interface), so set the cost explicitly when you want to control the path. LSA types 1 and 2 live inside the area, types 3 and 4 are generated by the ABR and type 5 (or 7, in an NSSA) carries external routes. Tip: when reading the database, look at the LSA type first, because it tells where the route came from.

Sources:

slides.title: OSPF authentication: from MD5 to HMAC-SHA
notes:
Authenticating OSPF stops an intruder router, or a misconfigured device, from injecting routes into the network. The type 1 simple password travels in the clear and only guards against mistakes; cryptographic authentication sends a digest of each packet and never the key. In 2007 the Enterasys equipment offered a simple password of up to eight characters and MD5; today the reference is the HMAC-SHA of RFC 5709, where HMAC-SHA-256 is mandatory for implementations of the specification. For the lab use SHA where the vendor supports it and MD5 only where there is no alternative. Tip: change the key with both sides ready and check the neighbor right afterwards, because a side with a different key makes the other discard every packet.

slides.title: OSPF: configuration and verification (2/2)
notes:
Side-by-side view of block B19. The full commands and the source of every line are on the vendor slides that follow.

• OSPFv2 defines three authentication types (AuType): 0 null, 1 simple password and 2 cryptographic; the original cryptographic method uses Keyed-MD5.
• RFC 5709 adds HMAC-SHA-1, -256, -384 and -512 to cryptographic authentication: HMAC-SHA-256 is mandatory and Keyed-MD5 is kept only for backward compatibility. Prefer SHA over MD5.
• RFC 7474 protects against replay attacks (inter-session and intra-session) when keys are configured manually, using extended sequence numbers.

slides.title: Lab: OSPF between the core and the uplink
notes:
This lab reuses the addressing from the static route lab: SW-CORE-01 has router-id 10.255.0.1 and talks to the uplink router on 10.0.12.0/30. Build the plain adjacency first and only then add authentication, redistribution and the default route, checking the neighbor at each step. The last two steps cause failures on purpose so that the class recognizes the symptoms: with the wrong key or a different Hello the neighbor never reaches Full. On platforms without a network type or passive interface (such as the C3), record the limitation and carry on with the rest. Tip: write down the time of each change, because the syslog in the next block lets you correlate the neighbor going down with the change you made.

slides.title: VRRP: virtual IP, election and preemption
notes:
The hosts keep pointing to a single gateway, 10.1.10.1, which is now a virtual address: the Active router answers ARP and forwards, and the other stays in Backup. The router with the highest priority wins the election; on a tie, the higher IP address wins. The address owner (priority 255) is a special case, and here neither switch is the owner because the real IPs are 10.1.10.2 and 10.1.10.3. With preemption on, which is the default, SW-CORE-01 takes the Active role back when it returns; turn preemption off if you prefer not to switch gateways again when it returns. Note that the current standard, RFC 9568, replaced the term Master with Active, while the 2007 guide still says master. Tip: use clearly different priorities, such as 110 and 100, so the election never depends on the address tie-break.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), p. 16-48 (PDF 526), address; p. 16-49 (PDF 527), priority; p. 16-51 (PDF 529), preempt (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: VRRP: timers and versions 2 and 3
notes:
This table shows what changed between the 2004 VRRPv2, which the 2007 equipment implemented, and the VRRPv3 in force. Version 3 covers IPv4 and IPv6 and measures the advertisement interval in centiseconds, but the default is still one second. The time for a Backup to declare the Active router down is three intervals plus a small delay that is smaller the higher the priority: with a 1 s interval and priority 100 that is about 3.6 s if the link is cut, and only the delay, about 0.6 s, when the Active shuts down in an orderly way and advertises priority 0. The current standard, RFC 9568 of April 2024, replaces RFC 5798, which had already replaced RFC 3768. Tip: check the same advertisement interval on both switches, because different intervals cause unstable role changes.

slides.title: VRRP on the Enterasys CLI (C3)
notes:
On the C3, VRRP is configured in its own mode. Enter router mode with router vrrp, create the session for the VLAN and VRID, enter the virtual IP and the priority, and only at the end enable the session. The last number of the address command says whether the switch owns the address: since 10.1.10.1 is not a real address of either one, we use 0 on both. The advertisement interval is in seconds and must be the same on routers with the same VRID. The guide writes the preempt command without the word vlan on the syntax line, but the example uses it; follow the example. Tip: configure and enable the switch that will be the Backup first and the higher priority one last, to watch the election happen in show ip vrrp.

slides.title: VRRP (2/2)
notes:
Side-by-side view of block B20. The full commands and the source of every line are on the vendor slides that follow.

• The current VRRP is RFC 9568 (April 2024, VRRPv3 for IPv4 and IPv6), which obsoletes RFC 5798; that one had already obsoleted RFC 3768 (VRRPv2). It uses IP protocol 112 and multicast 224.0.0.18.
• The IPv4 virtual MAC is 00-00-5E-00-01-{VRID}; for the lab's VRID 10 it is 00-00-5E-00-01-0A. The default priority is 100 and 255 marks the IPvX address owner.
• Preemption is on by default (Preempt_Mode = True) and the default advertisement interval is 100 centiseconds (1 s); the address owner always preempts.
