slides.title: Lab: redundant gateway on VLAN 10
notes:
This lab uses two core switches and a host on VLAN 10. Start by checking the state before causing failures: SW-CORE-01, with priority 110, must be the Active router. Cut the Active router's link and measure the switchover time with a continuous ping, expecting about 3.6 s with a 1 s interval; then repeat by shutting VRRP down in an orderly way to see a much faster switchover. Compare the MAC the host learned in its ARP table with the virtual MAC from the standard, where VRID 10 appears as 0A. Tip: repeat the test with preemption off to see that SW-CORE-02 stays Active when SW-CORE-01 comes back.

Sources:
[1] RFC 9568, Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) Version 3 for IPv4 and IPv6, 6.1 Parameters per Virtual Router (Skew_Time, Active_Down_Interval); 6.4.2 Backup (priority 0); 7.3 Virtual Router MAC Address. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9568.txt

slides.title: ACL: first match and implicit deny
notes:
The packet runs through the rules in order and the first one that matches decides: permit or deny. The lab rules start with the most specific one, which permits SSH from VLAN 10 to VLAN 99, then deny everything else to VLAN 99 and finally permit the rest of the traffic. Because the last rule permits everything, the implicit deny at the end of the list never acts in this ACL; in a list without that final rule, everything not permitted would be denied. If we swap the first two rules, SSH becomes denied, because the rule that denies everything matches first. Tip: always put specific rules before general ones and keep a console session open when applying an ACL in production.

Sources:
[1] Cisco IOS XE Security Configuration Guide: Access Control Lists, Creating an IP Access List and Applying It to an Interface, Information About Creating an IP Access List and Applying It to an Interface. https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/ios-xml/ios/sec_data_acl/configuration/xe-16/sec-data-acl-xe-16-book/sec-create-ip-apply.html

slides.title: ACL: standard or extended, wildcard or prefix
notes:
The standard ACL looks only at the source address, and the extended one looks at protocol, source, destination and port; on the C3 the numbering is 1 to 99 and 100 to 199. The wildcard is the inverse of the subnet mask: a 0 bit must match and a 1 bit is ignored, so 0.0.0.255 is equivalent to a /24. The table shows the equivalences that appear most in the lab, such as the /30 of the uplink link and the /24 of the VLANs. A packet filter decides only on fields of the IP and transport headers; RFC 3234 contrasts such stateless firewalls with stateful ones, which also reassemble IP fragments. Because the standard ACL sees only the source, applying it near the source would block that source toward every destination, which is why it usually sits near the destination; this is a consequence of what the ACL examines, not a rule from a standard. Tip: convert the wildcard to a prefix in your head before applying the rule.

slides.title: ACL on the Enterasys CLI (C3)
notes:
On the C3, ACLs are numbered and exist only in router mode: 1 to 99 are standard, 100 to 199 are extended. The 2007 guide places the port operator right after the source, and the DFE guide example shows that in that position the port is the source port; that is why the legacy example permits TCP from VLAN 10 to VLAN 99 without restricting port 22, which the modern lab does restrict. Application is inbound only on the routed interface, which fits the MGMT-PROTECT design. The show access-lists output lists the numbered entries, but the guide example shows no counters; the DFE offers the log option to send hits to syslog. Tip: when editing a numbered ACL use insert, replace and move instead of deleting it, so the interface is not left without a rule in the middle of the change.

slides.title: Lab: protect the management VLAN
notes:
The goal is to see the ACL working and also failing. Build the three rules in the order of the diagram, apply it inbound on VLAN 10 and test SSH and other protocols from a host in that VLAN to a host in VLAN 99. Then swap the first two rules on purpose and watch SSH being denied, to fix the idea that the first matching rule decides. Where the platform shows hit counters, use them to confirm which rule caught the traffic; where it does not, as in the C3 show access-lists, confirm by the test result or by log. Tip: run each test from the host, not from the switch itself, because traffic generated by the switch may not go through the interface ACL.

slides.title: Syslog: from device to server
notes:
The message leaves the device with a priority number in angle brackets, calculated as facility times 8 plus the severity; for example, local4 with severity notice gives 165, the same value that appears in the C3 buffer. The simplest transport is UDP on port 514, which does not acknowledge receipt and can therefore lose messages without telling anyone. To protect the content and prove who sent it, TLS on TCP port 6514 is used. Time also matters: the modern RFC 5424 format comes from RFC 3339 and accepts the time zone, while the old BSD format of RFC 3164 carries only local month, day and time, with no year or zone. Tip: synchronize every device with NTP before relying on logs to correlate events.

slides.title: Syslog: the eight severities
notes:
The eight severities run from emergency, when the system is unusable, down to debug. RFC 5424 numbers them 0 to 7, and the 2007 C3 guide numbers them 1 to 8, so the same name has a number one higher in the legacy: informational is 6 in the RFC and 7 on the C3. This difference is a classic trap, so always check the name as well as the number. The RFC calls the facility and severity values non-normative but widely used, and defines facilities 0 to 23, of which local0 to local7 are 16 to 23. Tip: in the lab we send the informational level, which shows login and port state change events without flooding the server with debug output.

slides.title: Syslog: formats and transports
notes:
This table compares the three ways of carrying syslog to the server. UDP on port 514 is the simplest and the most common on older devices, but RFC 5426 warns that messages can be lost without notice, and an attacker can discard them to hide activity. Syslog over plain TCP is described in RFC 6587, a historical document: it has no standardized port, and the IESG does not recommend using it because it cannot provide strong security. The recommended way is TLS on port 6514, updated by RFC 9662, which changes the mandatory cipher suites and asks for TLS 1.3 to be preferred when supported. Tip: if a device only speaks UDP, put the collector on the same management network and protect that path, instead of sending logs across the user network.

slides.title: Syslog on the Enterasys CLI (C3)
notes:
On the C3, the syslog server is one row of a table of up to eight entries, and the set logging server command defines the address, facility, severity and port of each. Remember that the guide severity runs 1 to 8, so the informational level of our lab is 7. The guide defaults are facility local4 and port 514. The show logging buffer command shows only the last 256 messages, which is why the central server is indispensable. The time of the messages depends on the clock: the C3 uses the SNTP client, here pointed at the lab server 192.0.2.123. Tip: after configuring, force an event such as a login and confirm on the server that the message arrived with the expected facility.

slides.title: SNMP: manager, agent and notifications
notes:
The drawing shows the classic split: on one side the manager, the monitoring station 192.0.2.60, and on the other the agent, which runs on SW-CORE-01. The manager sends read and write requests to UDP port 161 of the agent, and the agent answers. When an event happens, such as a link going down, the agent sends a notification on its own to UDP port 162 of the receiver. The notification can be a trap, which has no confirmation, or an inform, which the receiver acknowledges with a response. Tip: use inform for events that must not be lost, and remember that even so the standard says there is no guarantee of delivery.

slides.title: SNMP: v1, v2c and v3
notes:
Versions 1 and 2c identify the manager only by a text called community, which travels in the clear; RFC 3410 says these versions are fundamentally insecure and were declared Historic. Version 3 adds user, authentication and encryption per message, and is the only one that is part of the standard set STD 62. RFC 3410 itself expects vendors and users to keep using v1 and v2c, and RFC 3584 describes how the three versions coexist. In the lab, the read-only v2c community appears only as a discouraged example. Tip: if v2c cannot be avoided, limit the community to read access, restrict the address of the manager and do not reuse it on more than one device.

slides.title: SNMPv3: security levels and algorithms (USM)
notes:
USM, the security model of SNMPv3, works with three levels: no authentication and no privacy, authentication without privacy, and authentication with privacy. The authPriv level is the one we use in the lab, because the user proves who it is and the content travels encrypted. In 2007 the available algorithms were HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA for authentication and 56-bit DES for privacy; the C3 guide shows exactly that combination. Later came AES-128 in RFC 3826 and the HMAC-SHA-2 family in RFC 7860, where SHA-256 is mandatory for implementations of the specification. Tip: before configuring, check in the device manual which algorithms it accepts, because the manager and the agent must use the same ones.

slides.title: SNMP: MIB, OID and notifications
notes:
Everything SNMP reads or changes is an object in a MIB, and each object has a numeric address called an OID, written as a sequence of numbers separated by dots. The classic example is 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1, the system description: iso, org, dod, internet, mgmt, mib-2, system group, object 1. SNMPv3 access control uses views: a group gets a read view, a write view and a notify view, and each view is a set of included or excluded subtrees. Notifications leave along the path that the C3 guide shows, in which the notify entry points to a tag, the tag points to a target address and the address points to the security parameters. Tip: to audit, run an snmpwalk from the root 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 and check that the device answers only what the view allows.

slides.title: RMON: remote monitoring (2007 heritage)
notes:
RMON extends SNMP with additional MIBs, which generate a much richer set of data about network usage. The device itself measures statistics and history, compares values with thresholds and generates an event when a threshold is crossed. RFC 2819 defines the MIB, with ten groups, all optional, and the 2007 C3 implements six of them: statistics, history, alarm, event, filter and packet capture. The results kept in the device are read by the management station over SNMP. Tip: the alarm group lets you generate an event when a counter, such as CRC errors, passes a value.

[2] RFC 2819, Remote Network Monitoring Management Information Base (STD 59), Abstract; 2.3 Structure of MIB. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2819.txt

slides.title: SNMPv3 on the Enterasys CLI (C3)
notes:
On the C3, SNMPv3 is assembled from pieces that fit together. The user nms receives the authentication and privacy passwords, the group NMS-RO gathers that user, the view defines what can be read, and the access command links the group to the view with the required security level. For notifications, targetparams says which user and level to send with, notify creates the tag and the type, and targetaddr points to the receiver 192.0.2.60 and ties everything together by the tag. The guide allows at most 32 characters in the target names and requires at least 8 characters in the passwords. Tip: after configuring, generate an event such as an unplugged cable and confirm on the receiver that the notification arrived with the expected user.

slides.title: RADIUS: the path of a management login
notes:
Follow the path in the drawing. The administrator netadmin opens an SSH session to SW-CORE-01, and the switch, which plays the role of network access server, builds an Access-Request with the user name and a password hidden by an MD5-based calculation and the shared secret. The RADIUS server 192.0.2.10 looks up its database and answers Access-Accept or Access-Reject, and if the server does not answer the switch re-sends and may try an alternate server. The shared secret never travels over the network, so it must be identical on both sides. On the C3, the server can return the management level of the user in the Filter-ID attribute, with the values ro, rw or su. Tip: keep the secret in a password vault and use a different secret for each device.

slides.title: RADIUS or TACACS+?
notes:
The comparison shows that each protocol has its typical use: the RADIUS RFC speaks of a network access server authenticating links and users, and the TACACS+ RFC highlights device administration. RADIUS uses UDP and hides the user password with an MD5-based calculation, while TACACS+ uses TCP and obfuscates the packet body with the shared secret. RFC 8907 is frank: this is obfuscation, not encryption, and an attacker with access to the data stream must be assumed able to read and modify the packets. The strong point of TACACS+ for management is that it separates authentication, authorization and accounting, which helps to authorize and record each command in a session. To protect the channel there is RFC 9887, which uses TLS 1.3 with TACACS+, and the variants of RADIUS over TLS, which are still experimental. Tip: RFC 8907 requires limiting access to known clients and controlling the security of the whole path, so keep the server on a management network.

[3] RFC 8907, The Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) Protocol, 1. Introduction; 3.4 Connection; 4.5 Data Obfuscation; 7 Accounting; 10.1 General Security of the Protocol. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8907.txt

slides.title: RADIUS on the Enterasys CLI (C3)
notes:
On the C3 the RADIUS configuration is short, but the order matters. First register the server with index, address, port 1812 and secret, then adjust the timeout and enable the client, and only then check with show radius. The guide warns that the client can only be enabled after the server is online and configured with the same secret. The last step is the management-access realm, which forces every management access (Telnet, SSH, local management) through the server; with it, or with the any realm, the local admin account stops working on the console, Telnet and Local Management. Tip: before activating the realm, open a second session and plan how to recover access if the server becomes unreachable.

slides.title: AAA: RADIUS and TACACS+ (1/2)
notes:
Side-by-side view of block B24. The full commands and the source of every line are on the vendor slides that follow.

• RADIUS: authentication on UDP 1812 (RFC 2865, Draft Standard), accounting on UDP 1813 (RFC 2866, Informational). Early deployments used 1645, which conflicts with another service.
• TACACS+ (RFC 8907, 2020) is Informational, uses TCP port 49 and only obfuscates the body with an MD5 pad. RFC 9887 (Dec 2025, Proposed Standard) adds TLS 1.3 on TCP 300 and retires the obfuscation.
• RADIUS over TLS (RFC 6614, TCP port 2083) is Experimental. RFC 9765 (April 2025, Experimental) defines RADIUS/1.1, which drops the shared secret and removes MD5-based methods.

slides.title: IPv4 multicast: the address blocks
notes:
Every IPv4 multicast address starts with the four bits 1110, which gives the range 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255, or 224.0.0.0/4. Inside it some blocks have their own role: 224.0.0.0/24 is for local link control and never crosses a router, like OSPF on 224.0.0.5. 232.0.0.0/8 is the source-specific multicast block, and 239.0.0.0/8 is for administrative use within a domain, where the group 239.1.1.1 of our lab fits. One more detail often surprises people: the Ethernet address uses only 23 of the 28 significant bits of the group, so different groups can land on the same MAC address. Tip: when choosing groups for an application, avoid the control blocks 224.0.0.0/24 and 224.0.1.0/24.

slides.title: IGMP: the three versions
notes:
IGMP is the conversation between the receiver and the router of its local network. In version 1 the router asks all hosts at 224.0.0.1 and the receivers answer with reports. Version 2 adds the leave message, which allows the stream to stop quickly, and a querier election in which the router with the lowest IP address wins. Version 3 adds source filtering, which is what source-specific multicast requires from hosts, and sends reports to 224.0.0.22. The 2007 C3 runs version 2 by default and accepts 1, 2 or 3. Tip: if the router speaks IGMPv3 and the snooping switch only understands IGMPv2, RFC 4541 foresees groups being flooded or cut off, and the way out is to adjust the router version or disable snooping.

slides.title: IGMP snooping: deliver only to those who asked
notes:
In the drawing, the querier 10.1.10.2 asks who wants group 239.1.1.1 and ports 1 and 3 answer with reports, while port 2 stays silent. The switch learns and starts sending the group only to ports 1 and 3, in addition to the port that leads to the router. RFC 4541 describes the rules: IGMP reports go only to router ports, packets for 224.0.0.x always go to all ports, and a group entry needs an expiry time, because the switch cannot rely only on the leave message. On the C3 the feature is turned on globally and then port by port. Tip: if a receiver stops getting the stream after a few minutes, first check that there is an active querier on the VLAN, because without queries the reports are no longer renewed.

slides.title: PIM-SM: the delivery tree and the rendezvous point (RP)
notes:
Follow the tree in the drawing. The receiver's router, the DR, sends a (*,G) Join towards the RP, and the joins from all receivers form the shared tree rooted at the RP. The source does not need to know anyone: its router encapsulates the packets in Register messages and sends them to the RP, which distributes them over the tree. Later, the receiver's router may move to the shortest path to the source with an (S,G) Join, avoiding the detour through the RP. In the lab the RP is the loopback 10.255.0.1 of SW-CORE-01, configured statically, and the RFC mentions other ways to discover it: bootstrap or embedded-RP. Tip: the RP is a critical point, so use a loopback address and confirm that every router in the domain points to the same RP.

slides.title: DVMRP: flood-and-prune multicast (legacy)
notes:
RFC 1075, from 1988, introduced DVMRP when no routing protocol for multicast between networks was yet available, and it works by flooding: the router sends the packet out of every path except the one back to the source, and a router with no members sends a prune up the tree. From time to time it refloods to reach new receivers. The C3 guide says DVMRP suffices where members are many and bandwidth is plentiful, and that PIM-SM suits sparse members and limited bandwidth. RFC 1075 itself treats the protocol as experimental and does not recommend implementing it. Tip: if you find DVMRP in an old network, plan the migration to PIM-SM and remember that both features required an advanced license on the C3.

slides.title: Multicast on the Enterasys CLI (C3)
notes:
On the C3, multicast has two layers of commands. In switch mode, IGMP snooping is turned on globally and then on ports, and show igmpsnooping mfdb shows the forwarding table with the MAC address of each group. In router mode, ip igmp turns IGMP on globally and ip igmp enable turns it on each interface, such as the VLAN 10 one. PIM-SM requires an advanced license, can only be turned on after IGMP is active, and the static RP takes an address, group and mask, which for all multicast is 224.0.0.0 with 240.0.0.0. Tip: after configuring, join a group from a receiver and check, in this order, the mfdb, show ip igmp groups and the PIM neighbors.

slides.title: Multicast: IGMP snooping and PIM (2/2)
notes:
Side-by-side view of block B25. The full commands and the source of every line are on the vendor slides that follow.

• Current IGMPv3 is RFC 9776 (STD 100, Mar 2025), obsoleting RFC 3376 and updating IGMPv2 (RFC 2236). MLDv2 is RFC 9777 (STD 101), obsoleting RFC 3810. IGMPv3 reports go to 224.0.0.22.
• IGMP snooping is not a standardized protocol: there is only RFC 4541 (May 2006), Informational, which "does not specify an Internet standard of any kind".
• PIM-SM is RFC 7761 (STD 83, March 2016), which obsoletes RFC 4601; it uses IP protocol 103 and group 224.0.0.13. A PIM router MUST support static group-to-RP mappings, like the lab's static RP.

slides.title: Lab: multicast with IGMP snooping and PIM-SM
notes:
The goal is to see multicast reach only those who asked for it, first at layer 2 and then between routers. Start with snooping and the querier on VLAN 10, join a group with each receiver and follow the group table. Only then turn on PIM-SM on VLAN 10 and the uplink, with the static RP on loopback 10.255.0.1 of SW-CORE-01, and send the stream from the source behind the uplink. The last step turns snooping off on purpose so that the class sees the stream flood the ports without receivers. Tip: use a simple traffic generator and a receiver with packet capture, because seeing the packet arrive or not arrive teaches more than reading the table.

slides.title: Troubleshooting: climb the layers, bottom-up
notes:
The ladder goes from the cable up to the application, and the rule is to climb one step at a time. At the base are the physical medium and the link, where the IEEE 802.3 standard defines the physical layer and media access control, and where VLANs, STP and LACP live. Above comes the network layer of the Internet architecture, which gathers IP, ICMP and IGMP, and OSPF and VRRP also travel over IP. Last come transport and application, where syslog, SNMP and RADIUS travel over UDP. Tip: when two symptoms seem unrelated, look for the cause in the lowest layer that appears in both.

slides.title: Troubleshooting: the six-step method
notes:
This is the working method we use in the labs, and it does not come from a standard: it is a simple discipline. First define the problem precisely, saying what the symptom is, who is affected and since when. Then collect facts, such as versions, logs with time, configuration and topology, and isolate the cause by climbing the layers. Only then fix it, changing one thing at a time and knowing how to go back. Finally verify with the same test that failed and document the cause, the fix and what prevents a repeat. Tip: write down the time of each change, because the central log lets you correlate the change with the effect.

Sources:
[1] LAN Switch Operations and Maintenance course material (original 2007 edition and 2026 edition, Rodolfo Nützmann): the course's own teaching content; the technical statements and commands used are on the corresponding slides, with their official sources

slides.title: Common symptoms and where to start
notes:
The table gathers the symptoms the class will see in the labs and links each one to the most likely cause according to the standards we studied. An OSPF neighbor that does not reach Full usually has a different key or timers, but remember that on a LAN the 2-Way state between routers that are neither DR nor BDR is normal. In VRRP, two active routers mean they stopped hearing each other, and RFC 9568 reminds us that the protocol has no authentication. When SNMPv3 does not answer, the USM counters tell whether the problem is the user, the authentication or the encryption, and when RADIUS times out it is worth checking that the server knows the client and the secret. Tip: always confirm the time and time zone of the logs before comparing events across devices.

slides.title: Troubleshooting toolkit
notes:
Side-by-side view of block B26. The full commands and the source of every line are on the vendor slides that follow.

• LLDP is IEEE 802.1AB (EtherType 0x88CC). The 2016 edition is superseded by 802.1AB-2026 (approved 2026-09-25). Default interval 30 s; TTL = interval x multiplier + 1 (121 s for 30 s and 4).
• DOM for SFP/SFP+ is in SFF-8472 (Rev 12.5a, 2026-01-16), at I2C address A2h: temperature, voltage, TX bias, TX and RX power, plus alarm and warning thresholds.
• Optical power is reported in 0.1 µW steps (0 to 6.5535 mW, about -40 to +8.2 dBm), accuracy +/-3 dB. pcap and pcapng have no RFC, only IETF OPSAWG drafts.

slides.title: Before opening a case: what to collect
notes:
A well-opened case is solved in hours, and a vague case often goes around for days. The list has seven items: device identification, the support output with the configuration, logs with the right time, the topology and recent changes, the time and impact, the steps to reproduce and the support entitlement. The Matrix DFE show support command illustrates the idea well, because it runs versions, hardware, VLANs, logs, counters, STP, routes, ARP, utilization and configuration at once and saves everything to a file. Remove passwords and secrets before sending any file. Tip: Cisco, for example, asks for a valid service contract and suggests attaching a screen recording to help reproduce the problem, and each vendor has its own procedure.

[1] Cisco Support (service contract and support case information), Support landing page (service contract; support case). https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/index.html
[2] Enterasys Matrix DFE-Platinum and Diamond Series Configuration Guide, Firmware 5.41.xx, P/N 9033800-14 (March 2007), p. 2-158 and 2-159 (PDF 184-185): 2.2.13.1 show support (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)

slides.title: Data collection on the Enterasys CLI
notes:
These are the commands a 2007 technician used to build the evidence folder for a case. The version and hardware identify the device, utilization shows CPU and memory, the system time confirms whether the clock is right, and the log buffer holds the last 256 messages, which is little for an old incident. The configuration can be displayed or written to a file. On the Matrix DFE, show support does almost everything at once and saves the result, as in the slot1/support3.txt example. Tip: save each file with the device name and the date and time of the collection, so support knows exactly which moment it refers to.

slides.title: Final lab A: redundant core
notes:
This is the first of two final labs and it joins everything the course built about layer 2 and layer 3. Build the base before routing: VLANs and trunk, then LACP between the cores and RSTP with SW-CORE-01 as root, because Spanning Tree treats the LAG as a single port. Only then turn on VRRP on VLAN 10, with priorities 110 and 100, and OSPF in area 0 with authentication. The final test is failure: cut SW-CORE-01's link and measure about 3.6 s on the continuous ping for SW-CORE-02 to take over, then remove one of the two LAG cables and see that traffic continues. Tip: verify each layer before climbing to the next, using the troubleshooting ladder from the previous block. At the end, save each switch configuration named after the lab and the bench number, as in the original 2007 course rule.

slides.title: Final lab B: protection and management
notes:
The second final lab puts protection and observability on top of the core you built in lab A. The first step is the clock, because the log only helps investigation if the time is right on the three switches. Next come the MGMT-PROTECT ACL, which must permit SSH from VLAN 10 to VLAN 99 and deny the rest, syslog, SNMPv3 and, last, RADIUS, the only step that can lock you out. The three failure tests are there to recognize symptoms: the ping denied by rule 20, the SNMPv3 query with a wrong password and the login when the RADIUS server does not answer. Tip: keep a console session open throughout the lab and only require RADIUS after validating a test user. At the end, save each configuration named after the lab and the bench number.

slides.title: Final assessment (1/3): Ethernet, switching, STP and addressing
notes:
The final assessment repeats the eight questions from the start of the course and adds four about this day's topics, so that learning can be compared. Run it in the same format as the initial one, ungraded and anonymous, with about fifteen minutes for the twelve questions. This first part revisits Ethernet, switching, Spanning Tree and addressing. After each answer, read the explanation aloud, because it cites the standard that supports the correct answer. Tip: add up the correct answers per question and compare with the initial assessment to find which topics need reinforcement.

Answer key:
1. B: RFC 894 sets 1500 octets as the maximum IP datagram over Ethernet; 46 octets is the minimum of the data field, padded if needed.
2. B: Frames to an unknown destination MAC are flooded like broadcasts, and the source MAC is associated with the port it arrived on (RFC 4762, 4.1 and 4.2).
3. D: The highest priority (lowest numerical value) wins the root election; on a tie, the lowest MAC address wins (C3 guide, 6-17).
4. C: RFC 1918 reserves 10/8, 172.16/12 (172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255) and 192.168/16; 172.32.0.1 is outside them.

Sources:
[1] SecureStack C3 Stackable Switches Configuration Guide, Firmware 1.00.xx, P/N 9034313-03 (June 2007), p. 6-17 (PDF p. 251), set spantree priority, Usage (not published online any more; copy in the author's archive)
[2] RFC 894, A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams over Ethernet Networks (STD 41), Frame Format. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc894.txt
[3] RFC 4762, Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) Using LDP Signaling, 4.1 Flooding and Forwarding; 4.2 Address Learning. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4762.txt
[4] RFC 1918, Address Allocation for Private Internets (BCP 5), 3. Private Address Space. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918.txt

slides.title: Final assessment (2/3): addressing, routing and management
notes:
This second part repeats the last four questions from the start of the course: IP addressing, route selection, TTL and SSH. These are the concepts behind every lab of the day, so it is worth hearing who changed their answer since the morning of the first day. If most of the class still misses the most-specific-route question, go back to the Module 03 routing table and redo the example. Tip: ask a student to explain the right answer in their own words before reading the explanation.

Answer key:
5. C: A /24 spans 256 addresses (RFC 4632, 3.1) and a host number of all zeros or all ones is not allowed (RFC 1122, 3.2.1.3): that leaves 254.
6. C: The router uses the most specific matching route (the longest prefix): 10.1.10.0/24, via R3 (RFC 1812, 2.2.5.2 and 5.2.4.3).
7. B: The packet must be discarded and, unless the destination is multicast, the router must send ICMP Time Exceeded, code 0, to the source (RFC 1812, 5.3.1); the type is 11 (RFC 792).
8. A: RFC 4253 describes the SSH transport layer with strong encryption, host (server) authentication and integrity protection; RFC 4251 summarizes the same.

Sources:
[1] RFC 4632, Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR) (BCP 122), 3.1 Basic Concept and Prefix Notation. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632.txt
[2] RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers (STD 3), 3.2.1.3 Addressing. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122.txt
[3] RFC 1812, Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers, 2.2.5.2 CIDR; 5.2.4.3 Next Hop Address (Longest Match); 5.3.1 Time to Live. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1812.txt
[4] RFC 792, Internet Control Message Protocol (STD 5), Time Exceeded Message. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc792.txt
[5] RFC 4253, The Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Protocol, 1. Introduction. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4253.txt
[6] RFC 4251, The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Architecture, Abstract. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4251.txt

slides.title: Final assessment (3/3): OSPF, VRRP, ACL and SNMPv3
notes:
The four new questions cover the topics that weighed most today: OSPF 2-Way, VRRP preemption, ACL rule order and the SNMPv3 security level. All of them use the lab values, which helps the class connect theory to what was configured. On the ACL question, ask the student to say aloud which rule is consulted first, because that is where most people miss. Tip: use the questions the class missed most as the outline for the final five minutes of review before the satisfaction survey.

Answer key:
9. B: On broadcast networks adjacencies form only with the DR and the BDR; between the others the neighbor stays in 2-Way, which is normal (RFC 2328, 10.4).
10. B: With Preempt_Mode true, a higher-priority Backup that starts or restarts takes over from the lower-priority Active Router (RFC 9568, 6.1 and 6.4.2). The IP only breaks ties between equal priorities.
11. B: Rule 10 only matches TCP port 22. Rule 20 matches any IP to VLAN 99, and the first matching rule decides: the ping is denied and rule 30 is never consulted.
12. C: authPriv combines authentication and privacy (RFC 3411, 3.4.3); SHA authenticates (RFC 3414) and AES-128 encrypts (RFC 3826). The community belongs to v1 and v2c.

[3] RFC 9568, Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) Version 3 for IPv4 and IPv6, 6.1 Parameters per Virtual Router (Preempt_Mode); 6.4.2 Backup; 6.4.3 Active. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9568.txt
[4] RFC 3411, An Architecture for Describing Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) Management Frameworks (STD 62), 3.4.3 securityLevel. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3411.txt

[6] RFC 3826, The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Cipher Algorithm in the SNMP User-based Security Model, 1. Introduction; 1.1 Goals and Constraints. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3826.txt

slides.title: Satisfaction survey
notes:
Close the day with the satisfaction survey, on paper or as a form, and give about five minutes for each person to mark one option per row. The three criteria are the instructor, the material and the overall rating, and there is room for free comments. Step out of the room while the class answers, so the answers are frank. Tip: read the comments the same day and note what to change for the next class, because the memory of what worked or not is still fresh.

Sources:
[1] LAN Switch Operations and Maintenance course material (original 2007 edition and 2026 edition, Rodolfo Nützmann): the course's own teaching content; the technical statements and commands used are on the corresponding slides, with their official sources

slides.title: Closing
notes:
Close the day by recalling the common thread: we started with core redundancy, moved to protection and management, saw multicast and ended with the investigation method and the data collection for support. Remember that every topic had three layers, theory backed by standards, the historical 2007 CLI and the current CLI of the eight vendors, and that the labs always used the same addresses. Ask each person to keep the saved configurations named after the lab and the bench number. Take the chance to collect the remaining questions and agree on how the class will stay in touch with the [Partner] or the instructor. Tip: suggest one lab to repeat at home the following week, because spaced practice fixes what was learned.
